Especiolly able during the hot months. 40 Carl Breer and associates De Soto Airflowautomobile, Chrysler Corporation, 1934 The aim of this design by Breer, head of Research at Chrysler, was to parallel the popular success of other forms of streamlined transport such as the Douglas DC-3 aeroplane and the Pullman Company's City of Salina railway train.
Although not a great commercial success, perhaps due to its radical design, its streamlined form was adopted subsequently with far greater profit by other US manufacturers.
Much of its external detailing has an Art Deco flavour, and the interior includes chromium-plated tubular steel seat frames and marbled rubber floor mats. ![](images/ee7fab69d833d57906b7ff9cf721d1d03265d50bacfd2212f468346b6601d509.jpg) as Raymond Loewy or Norman Bel Geddes and portray them as the creators of modern mass culture'.6 As an anthropologist Miller was arguing for greater recognition of the transformation of goods in consumption as a means of understanding material culture, but even from a more conventional historical perspective undue emphasis on the individual is somewhat misleading.
Harold Van Doren in his 194o text, Industrial Design: A Practical Guide,7 stressed the importance of specialist collaboration as a means of achieving greater levels of effectiveness in the industrial design profession and suggested that a design team should include a designer, an engineer, a technical expert, a manufacturer, a merchandiser, and others with a knowledge of productionplanning and channels of distribution.
Indeed, in the 193os the offices of leading industrial designers were often quite sizeable: in 1934 Bel Geddes's office embraced design, drafting, modelling, and technical activities, employing about 3o with outside specialists being brought in as required; by 1937 Teague employed25; and by the end of the decade the flamboyant Loewy employed 6o.
None the less, although much of the literature of American industrial design has tended to emphasize the positive achievements of the emergent design profession, this was not a representative picture of the ways in which it was recognized by industry at the time.
Harold Van Doren, as late as 194o, was at pains to stress that the designer's position in industry was still tenuous,with the majority of manufacturers either unconvinced by, or unaware of, the efficacy of design as a business tool.
He related that many of them were unused to budgeting appropriately for the implementation of a design programme and expected immediate results rather than the necessity of investment in longer-term strategies. ## The mass media as stimuli for consumption Like the highly influential mail-order catalogue, the radio did much to bring about a greater homogeneity in national patterns of taste, especially with the erosion of regional barriers through the formation of national radio networks by NBC and CBS, respectively in 1926 and 1927.
During the 193os the cost of radio purchase had fallen dramatically and small (‘baby') radios retailed for as little as \$1o, making them widely accessible to most income groups.
Just as the Volksempfänger (‘People's Radio') was an important instrument of political propaganda in Germany under the Third Reich, so the radio in the United States was an important advertising medium for the goods and services of large-scale corporations.
By the later 193os radio advertising was highly significant in economic terms, and advertisers competed to promote all kinds of products at prime listening times.
These included radios themselves, gramophones, domestic appliances, kitchen equipment, home furnishings, and automobiles, as well as foodstuffs and other domestic goods.
Several writers⁸ have suggested strong parallels between the futurist Utopias of popularizing industrial designers such as Norman Bel Geddes and the visions described in contemporary science fiction, a genre which flourished in the late 192os and early 193os.
The same years also saw the birth of the popular comic-strip heroes Buck Rogers, Flash Gordon, and Superman, and magazines such as Hugo Gernsback's Amazing Stories, Astounding Stories, and Wonder Stories collectively sold more than 1.5 million issues per annum at the height of their popularity in 1935.
Concepts such as speed and change, and the exploration of the possibilities of new materials, together with the development of new modes of transport and appliances were also common to both the more extravagant futures portrayed by Bel Geddes and many science-fiction writers, illustrators, and film makers.
There ## 41 Staubsauger Champion vacuum cleaner, Type OK, Holland, late 1930s The dramatic shape of this chromium-plated,streamlined vacuum cleaner reveals the extent to which American inspired styling had permeated European markets, with the fascination for the aerodynamic forms of contemporary transport designs permeating the domestic arena. ![](images/2a6b8fbd04d4463ae4de37734039680af4639bef54c14882296a50ad9a413646.jpg) was in addition a mutual faith in the power of technology as a means of transforming society for the better.
In similar vein in the early 193os, in the wake of the Wall Street Crash, the American Technocratic Party briefly commanded public interest through its emphasis on scientists and engineers as the potential agents of future national prosperity rather than those associated with the discredited business and financial sectors.
Technological Utopian visions continued to be drawn to the public attention by events such as the Chicago Century of Progress Exhibition of 1933/4 which attracted a total of $4 8 , 7 6 9 , 2 2 7$ visitors over the two seasons of its opening, and the very much larger, in terms of site, New York World's Fair of 1939/4o which enjoyed 44,932,978 visitors.
The original ambitions of the Chicago Century of Progress Exhibition were thwarted by the collapse of the economy, since few foreign countries were in a position to participate.
The National Research Council, however, was able to organize a coherent exhibition on the theme of science, demonstrating both past achievements and future possibilities.
The sheer volume of visitors attested to the Exhibition's popularity, and the general public were able to wonder at marvels such as the photo-electric cell, to inspect G.
F.
Keck's House of Tomorrow of steel frame and glass walls built around a central core containing utilities, complete with aeroplane hangar and garage, and to travel one-third of a mile on the Sky Ride in double-decker rocketcars'suspended between two 628 feet tall towers.
In the Exhibition's second season the public were able to view the latest streamlined trains, Union Pacific's M-1o,ooo (later renamed The City of Salina) and Burlington's Zephyr.
The dramatic streamlined forms of both resulted from the exploration of the dramatic possibilities of new, lightweight materials and constructional techniques and offered new standards of comfort and design.
Vividly catching the public imagination, both trains underwent extensive national tours and did much to transform railway-locomotive and rolling-stock design andstimulate popular interest in the streamlining of a wide range of consumer durables during the rest of the decade.
The New York World's Fair of 1939/40, centred on the theme of 'Design for Tomorrow', provided an unrivalled opportunity for industrial designers to harness themselves to the marketing ambitions of the larger American corporations since, as Walter Dorwin Teague remarked in 1939, they weresupposed to understand public taste and be able to speak in the popular tongue, and because as a profession they are bound to disregard traditional forms and solutions and think in terms of today and tomorrow'.9 The main themes of the World's Fair echoed the major developments which had been taking place in the 193os: transportation, science, and communications.
On display were numerous examples of science-fiction as popularist ![](images/7624ad4544ad5a8c492d965a246e86ff48fb048d3de71cca276eadfde227ace5.jpg) ## 42 'Battle of the Centuries' dishwashing contest between Mrs Drudge and Mrs Modern (using a 1940 Westinghouse dishwasher) at the New York World's Fair, 1939/40 The Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company did much to draw the crowds into its building with exhibits such as a seven foot robot Elektro and his robotic dog, Sparko.
The 'Battle of the Centuries' was a similarly sensationalized piece of theatre.
The apparent social utopianist 'World of Tomorrow' theme of the Fair provided large-scale American corporations with an unparalleled opportunity to situate themselves as powerful economic forces in the quest to stimulate consumer demand. entertainment as, for example, in theTransportation Zone, where visitors could view Raymond Loewy's Rocketport of the Future.
There, in son et lumière, travel from London to New York was portrayed in the form of a passenger rocket being fired from a gun, witha projected journey time of an hour.
Moreover, in the Westinghouse Building visitors could marvel at the seven-feet-high robot Elektro and his robotic dog Sparko responding to a variety of spoken commands.
Rather more down to earth in the specific promotion of domestic appliances, in the Fair's second season, visitors could follow Westinghouse's ‘Battle of the Centuries'in which a dishwashingcontest was held between Mrs Drudge, who washed by hand, and Mrs Modern, who used a 1940 model Westinghouse electric dishwasher [42].
Although a somewhat crude piece of marketing propaganda, many of the more large-scale and elaborate examples of exhibitions and displays mounted by the larger American corporations were ultimately little more than vehicles for the creation of a future public demand for new ranges of consumer goods, mediated through the agency of industrial designers.
Glimpses into the future were an important part of visitors'experience.
A notable exhibit was HenryDreyfuss's futuristic vision of Democracity, an imagined world of 2o39 which was seen daily by 8,00o visitors; in the Consolidated Edison Building visitors could see Walter Dorwin Teague's and FrankJ.
Roorda's 'City of Light', the world's largest diorama, which portrayed the whole extent of New York from Westchester to Coney Island undergoing in the space of 12 minutes the changes in lighting experienced in 24 hours; inside the Ford Motor General Motors Exhibit at the New York World's Fair 1939/40, showing envisaged street scene of 1960 with General Motors buses and cars A major element of the General Motors 'Highways and Horizons' exhibit at the NYWF was Bel Geddes's Futurama.
One of the most popular draws of the Fair, it featured a panoramic, futuristic vision of the world of 1960 which visitors viewed from moving chairs, as if from a low flying aircraft.
Emerging from this seemingly vast perspective, visitors emerged on to this full-scale simulation of a street intersection of 1960 with segregated traffic and pedestrian flows.
Needless to say, this particular 'World of Tomorrow' featured exclusively General Motors products. ![](images/829167d466fe5fda57aee0b71d23112cb041421dd63c5bdc9998e4f9af45cfa6.jpg) Company Building visitors could view Teague's ‘Ford Cycle of Production', whilst outside they could road test Ford, Mercury, and Lincoln-Zephyr automobiles on the spiral ‘Road of Tomorrow'.
Visited by 5 million over the duration of the exhibition, the most popular exhibit was Norman Bel Geddes's Futurama which was located in the General Motors complex in the Transportation Zone.
It consisted of a projected world of 196o seen as if from a low-flying aircraft, with multi-lane highways carrying streamlined vehicles through a landscaped city of low and high-rise buildings, with views of zoned residential, commercial, and industrial districts, experimental farms, hydro-electric power plants, and spectacular countryside.
In reality visitors were carried 5oo metres by moving ramps and chairs at a simulated speed of 2oo miles per hour.
Visitors finally arrivedat a full-scale intersection of the 196o city [43], where road traffic was segregated from pedestrians, before being invited to inspect the latest General Motors products.
Numerous other leading American corporations also promoted themselves in a forward-looking way, including the Radio Corporation of America (RCA), which promoted the new, but still very expensive, medium of television which commenced commercial broadcasting on the opening day of the Fair.
Although many of these displays were promoted as glimpses of a future society in which American corporations, aided by the imaginative interpretations of industrial designers, helped to benefit society with a well-designed future they were perhaps more heavily gearedtowards increasedprofit margins and market share. ## Contemporary critiques of industrial culture A number of historians have drawn attention to the critics of the ethos of mass-production in contemporary America.10Some critics looked back to the past as representing a simpler, more moral existence, contrasting modern capitalist commercial society with a ruralway of life.
The photographer Doris Ulman, for example, through her early 193os imagesof the communities of the Appalachian mountains focused attention on the values inherent in folk' culture, sustained by craftsmen and women working within their own cultural traditions.
However, other more strident voices launched more direct attacks on contemporary industrial culture in the United States.
Henry Ford, whose assembly-line techniques were increasingly widely applied in factories throughout the industrialized world, was a particular target of those who saw life in the USA as shaped by the spiritual dictatorship of machinery, warfare and magazines and newspapers of large circulation'.11 For example, in Brave New World of 1932 Aldous Huxley attacked wide-spread faith in the concepts of the large-scale and standardization which he saw as major ingredients of what he feared would become a loveless and emotionally arid society, a society in which Fordism was the dominant religion, with Ford replacingGod and Ford's autobiography the Bible.
The cinema also carried a number of anti-technological messages in films such as Fritz Lang's chilling vision of Metropolis of 1926, a hostile, futurist city in which its inhabitants were enslaved and dominated by technology; many of the sets were directly inspired by the Manhattan skyline which Lang had seen on a visit to New York in 1924.
Over a decade later, in Chaplin's Modern Times of 1936, the relentless drive for ever-increasing efficiency in the production line (which Chaplin had experienced at first-hand at the Ford Factory in Detroit) eventually resuited in the insanity of the worker.
There were also critics within the wider reaches of the design world, perhaps the most articulate of whom was Richard Buckminster Fuller.12 Very much opposed to what he saw as the complicity of industrial designers in the superficial styling and built-in obsolescence of an everincreasing range of consumer goods, he had sought increasingly to propose design solutions that derived maximum human advantage from the minimum use of materials and energy.
He wrote on this Dymaxion' theme and produced prototypes for his highly revolutionary Dymaxion cars (from 1933) and bathrooms (from 193o) [142], although for a variety of reasons these failed to find acceptance with manufacturers.
Unwilling to compromise his beliefs, he remained highly sceptical of the grandiose claims of the burgeoning industrial-design profession to be able to take on everything from a fountain pen to an ocean liner.
Fuller viewed industrial design as a close adjunct of advertising and marketing and, reflecting on such an outlook in the late 195os, he declared; industrial design is a very tarnished affair . . .
I assure you that no aircraft company will let an industrial designer through its engineering frontdoor.
Industrial designers are considered to be pure interior and exterior decorators.
And yet, I've listened to industrial designers assert that they designed the steamship, United States.
If you were to exhibit schematically all the items that the industrial designers created for the United States, you would have sailing down New York Harbour an array of window curtains, chairs, paint clouds and bric-à-brac floating in space, with nothing to really hold it together.
To assert that these men designed the United States could not have been more dishonest.13 ## The impact of European design American interest in European design in the interwar years was bolstered by a number of European immigrant designers including Joseph Urban and Paul Frankl from Austria, Gustav Jensen from Denmark, Peter Muller-Munk from Germany, George Sakier, William Lescaze, and Raymond Loewy from France, and Paul Lazlo from Hungary.
Furthermore the American Designers' Gallery and Contempora Inc. were both established in the later 192os in order to promote modern decorative arts and design in the United States, much along the lines of European groups such as the WienerWerkstätten and the Werkbunds in Austria and Germany or the Société des Artistes Décorateurs in France.
Although the activities of such American propagandist organizations were seriously curtailed by the Wall Street Crash of 1929 they did much to foster a new climate for modern design in the United States in the years leading up to the Second World War.
Far more significant, however, was the international Exposition des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels which was held in Paris in 1925. ## Paris 1925: luxury, elegance, and commerce As has been seen in connection with the New York World's Fair of 1939/4o, international exhibitions were important vehicles for the promotion of national interests, whether propagandist or economic, most particularly for the host nation, whose industries and national displays assumed the greatest significance.
The Paris Exposition des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels of1925 was very much a matter of French national prestige since its explicit aim was to re-establish her preeminence as the leading force in the decorative arts.
Even before the outbreak of hostilities in 1914 France's economic status in this respect had been increasingly called into question as a result of the growing international industrial competitiveness of other countries.
For various reasons—most particularly the intervention of the First World War—the idea of mounting an international exhibition to follow up the 19oo Paris Exposition Universelle was not realized until 1919 when it featuredas part of the French postwar programmeof industrial development and economic recovery.Sponsored by the Ministries of Commerce and Fine Arts, the projected postwar exhibition was intended to encourage the establishment of a modern design vocabulary that would blend traditional French expertise in the design of luxury goods with the realities of modern mass-production technology.
None the less, the kind of modernism embraced by the vast majority of French products and room settings was far from the ideas being discussed by Muthesius and others at the Deutscher Werkbund before the First World War.
Apart from the austere modernism of Le Corbusier's Pavillon de l'Esprit Nouveau (discussed in Chapter 2, see 28) a quality of unbridled luxuriousness and élitismcharacterized a significant proportion of the French exhibits, many of which were out of the financial reach of the everyday consumer.
As a result the exhibition engendered a considerable amount of criticism.
None the less, as will be discussed below, many of the stylistic characteristics on display, subsequently known as Art Deco, were widely influential in the United States, and made their presence firmly felt in many fields of design in Britain and elsewhere.
One of the pavilions at the Exposition which attracted most attention wasJacques-Emil Ruhlmann's Pavilion of a Wealthy Collector [44].
Even the title confirmed Ruhlmann's close links with high fashion, high prices, exclusivity, and a premium on craftsmanship rather than industry.
Lacquered furniture by Dunand, decorative iron railings by Edgar Brandt, a blue and pink carpet by Gaudissard, and the celebrated exoticism of Jean Dupas's oil painting The Parakeets all sustained such an impression.
As at the Paris 19oo internationalexhibition, some of the most memorable displays a quarter of a century later were located in the pavilions of the great Parisian department stores, all of which were situated on favourable sites.
Their presence in the French section together with the enticing Rue des Boutiques on the Pont Alexandre III, helped sustain the desired image of Paris as a city of shopping.¹⁴ This street contained forty shop displays of haute couture, fashion accessories, perfumes, and other luxury goods.
The lavish displays of the Parisian department stores were driven by their desire to capitalize on a growing public interest in contemporary design.
This spirit of commercial entrepreneurship had already brought about the establishment of their own design ateliers: Primavera'(under the directorship of René Guilleré and his wife Charlotte Chaucet-Guilleré) had been established at Printemps in 1912, La Maîtrise (under Maurice Dufrène) at Galeries Lafayette in 1921, Pomone (under Paul Follot) at Bon Marché in 1923, and Studium Louvre (under Étienne Kohlmann and Maurice Matet) at the Magasins du Louvre in 1924 [45].
The official desire to overwhelm visitors with the excellence of French decorative arts was revealed by the amount of space allocated to 44 Jacques-Emil RuhImann Interior of the Hotel d'un Collectioneur, Exposition des Arts Decoratifs et Industriels, Paris, 1925 This pavilion epitomized the underlying aim of the 1925 Exposition—to reassert French prestige in the decorative arts and crafts.
The luxurious display included the work of many of the leading French contemporary decorative artists as a counterpart to the many items of furniture designed by Ruhlmann himself.
A prominent figure in such work, with his own furniture workshops, he also designed textiles, carpets, and other elements for the creation of a complete ensemble. ![](images/c7c816e4de930a00b6b63017dab85a3cbcd5272f73a84112c421fa8856e19738.jpg) the French sections, which amounted to about two-thirds of the whole 57-acre site.
Many of the most dazzling French displays were located in the displays of the Société des Artistes Décorateurs.
Entitled Reception Rooms and Private Apartments of a French Embassy', it occupied twenty-five fully furnished rooms set round a three-sided courtyard.
The Smoking Room by Jean Dunand, with its Cubistinspired forms and decorative motifs, stepped silver ceiling set off against highlights of red lacquer, and wall facings of black lacquer, attracted considerable attention.
However, its relevance to the average consumer was restricted to glamorous reinterpretations in Hollywood film sets, modernistic cinema foyers, and other public spaces intended to impress their occupants [46], such as restaurants, the interiors of ocean liners [47], or the foyers of important business enterprises. ## 45 André Fréchet Lahalle and Lavard, reception hall for the Studium-Louvre Pavilion, Exposition des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels, Paris, 1925 Many of the qualities found in Ruhlmann's pavilion (44) are reflected here, but at more affordable prices.
The Studium-Louvre was one of the major Parisian department stores with its own decorating studios.
The 1925 Exposition offered them an unprecedented opportunity to show potential clients the fullest display of designs which could grace the fashionable Art Deco home. ## Paris 1925 and the United States Although not a participant at the 1925 Paris Exposition des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels,15the United States appointed a commission of over a hundred representatives drawn from a wide range of industries and institutions to visit it and report on the state of contemporary European design.
Charles Richards, Director of the American Association of Museums, headed the commission and subsequently organized a touring exhibition of designs drawn from the 1925 exhibition which was shown in nine museums in the USA, commencing with the Metropolitan Museum in New York.
Drawing on diverse sources such as Fauvism, Cubism, Purism, and African art, the Art Deco style was characterized by flat, geometric abstract motifs used in a decorative manner, often deriving from sunbursts, lightning flashes, fountains, flowers, and other organic forms.
Such abstract forms soon became fashionable, and the style was actively promoted by leading stores throughout the country, many of whom also mounted exhibitions.16 In New York, artists such as Erté and Raoul Dufy designed for the Amalgamated Silk and Onondaga Companies, and firms such as Cheney Brothers and F.
Schumacher & Co marketed French textiles alongside other ranges. ![](images/8ffe6ad83604f59af4eee6892ba73c38417858fe707148cf341bacc5335655d5.jpg) Architecture and interiors, particularly in terms of detailing such as metalwork, lettering and signage, lighting and the geometric patterning of floor and wall surfaces, brought the Deco style very much to the public eye in the major cities of North America.
In New York, William Van Alen's Chrysler Building of 1928-31, with itsdramatic stainless steel cladding and roofline, external geometric frieze of wheels, radiator caps, and abstracted eagles, and striking lobby interior typified most vividly a stylistic trend which manifested itself throughout Manhattan.
In Washington many Government buildings, particularly in the Federal Triangle, also adopted the style, which was equally widespread in the West, as in Los Angeles, or in the south, as in Miami Beach.
The Deco influence was also widely seen in interiors connected with the leisure and entertainment industries.
The Rockefeller Center complex in New York provided an almost unprecedented opportunity for the explorationof the Deco style, particularly in the interiors of Radio City Music Hall (RCMH).
The elaborative decorative schemes were overseen byDonald Deskey who did much to link European design with practice in the United States, having studied in Paris in the early 192os and visited the 1925 Exposition.
He collaborated with a number of leading American designers, painters, and sculptors in the design of the foyer, auditorium, smoking and powder rooms, and other public spaces, contributing designs for some of the wallpapers and cov- ## 46 Jaap Gidding Foyer of the Tuschinki Cinema, Amsterdam, 1918–21 Superficially Gidding's dramatic and highly colourful designs have much in common with the decorative ethos of contemporary French decorative arts and the glitz of 1920s Hollywood film sets.
However, the expressive possibilities afforded by the cinema's unified external and ornamental decorative schemes also had more in common with the expressive work of the Amsterdam School, a progressive strand of Dutch design opposed to the greater commitment to a modernist machine age aesthetic of contemporary De Stijl architects and designers. ![](images/3f71eb332221ebe6b55b111534ee7d50c086c446418523ddc090d653c9521a4d.jpg) 80 COMMERCE, CONSUMERISM, AND DESIGN ## 47 Stanislaw Brukalski Interior of the America Bar, on the ocean liner MS Bathory, 1936 The interior of this transatlantic liner reveals the gradual elision of the modernist and 'applied arts' factions in 1930s Polish design.
Here Brukalski, who had been involved in the more radically modern factions of Polish design in the later 1920s and early 1930s, perhaps acknowledged the more decorative tendencies of the nationalistic Ład group which drew heavily upon folk art motifs and patterns.
None the less, the overall ethos of the bar was more in line with wider international tendencies in the decorative arts, reflecting the dual role of the vessel as a national carrier serving an international clientele. ![](images/cadf94a60d32cfd698d1e3afc9d2294bd9aa0ac98207917fff815a6c7bec1026.jpg) erings, carpets, furniture, and lighting designs.
Many of the interiors exhibited a distinctly Deco (or Moderne as its American derivate was often referred to) flavour in their exploration of the decorative possibilities of aluminium, bakelite, mirrors, glass, lacquer, andeven gold-leafed ceilings, all of which were reminiscent of the work of the French artistes-décorateurs of the 192os from which such an outlook ultimately derived.
Just as the 1925 Paris Exposition was an important influence on RCMH, many of the more lavish ensembles can be seen to have exerted an influence on Hollywood film sets, which in turn did much to popularize the Deco style.
For example, Van Nest Polglase designed the set for the Paramount film The Magnificent Flirt of 1928which showed a number of interiors which were amongst the earliest examples of Art Deco on film.
Studio publicity of the time proclaimed that the film showed the latest idea in interior architecture for the modern home'.
Similar trends could be seen in many other film sets through the later 192os and 193os, including Richard Day's designs for MGM's The Kiss, starring Greta Garbo, of 1929 [48].
Furthermore, Cedric Gibbons, the leading Hollywood Art Director of the time, visited the 1925 exhibition, and its direct influence could be seen, in his design for the fountain scene from MGM's Our Blushing Brides of 193o.
By the end of the decade there were about 40 million regular cinema-goers, underlining its potency as a medium for influencing patterns of taste and the consumption of particular products and lifestyles. ## Wider patterns of taste: historical diversity Not only was film instrumental in the promotion of luxurious Art Deco settings; it also drew on a huge variety of styles, periods, and geographical origins, ranging from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome through to the Middle Ages, the Renaissance and the Elizabethan era, and onwards to the present day.
American cinemas themselves also took on a plethora of styles in their highly striking interiors, often competingfor effect with the elaborate celluloid fantasiesseen on screen.17 Stylistic diversity was also reflected in the homes, furniture, and furnishings ofthe majority of Americans.
Although they willingly embraced notions of contemporaneity in the streamlined forms of their domestic appliances, kitchen equipment, and automobiles, admired the strikingly modern designs for public transport systems as seen in aircraft such as the Douglas DC-3, trains such as Dreyfuss's Twentieth Century Limited or Loewy'sGreyhound bus, they generally looked to traditional styles in the decoration of their homes.
The ubiquitous mail-order catalogues of the period unequivocally underline this affirmation of the traditional in the home.
Manufacturers were generally conservative in their outlook, drawing on the past for commercial survival in the present, and consumers could purchase a variety of styles includingTudor, Queen Anne, Chippendale, and Louis XVI.
In their 1945 book Tomorrow's House: A Complete Guide to the Home-Builder, the modernist propagandistsGeorge Nelson and Henry Wright lamented the sentimental attachment of home-owners to the past.
Considering the ‘Home as a Psychological Fact'they wrote: Home, in the American dream, is a quaint little white cottage, shyly nestled in a grove of old elms or maples, bathed in the perfume of lilacs, and equipped with at least one vine-covered wall.18 They also drew attention to such characteristics as ‘a steep gabled roof', tiny dormers', 'shutters in soft blue or green', a replica of an oil lamp, wired for electricity', and ‘a four-poster bed'and concluded that if people pursued this dream they would get either a cheap imitation or an outrageously expensive fake'.
The period styles in which many houses were built in the 192os and 3os reflected a similar spirit of retrospection, although taking on a richer diversity and choice.
As will be considered in the following chapter, a number of these styles were identified as specifically American in their origins and were promoted by a number of organizations intent on lessening dependency on European models through the establishment of a distinctive American style.
For example, the restoration of Williamsburg in 1926, funded by the Rockefellers, reinforced interest in the Colonial style [133]; the Spanish Colonial style, deriving from traditions rooted in the Southwest, was also popular.
The English Style', replete with half-timbering and pitched roof, also ## 48 Cedric Gibbons/ Richard Day Art Deco set for the MGM film The Kiss, 1929 This film, which starred Greta Garbo and Anders Randolf, featured many striking decoinspired sets designed by Richard Day.
The geometric form and decoration of the chair in which Randolf is seated, the angular coffee table, the stepped form of the fireplace, and the decorative over-mantel decoration all betray a French influence.
However, this interest in geometric decorative motifs was also reflected in a growing contemporary interest in native American artefacts, qualities of which may be discerned in the sofa covering to the right. ![](images/5e06fbfe009eb2bf133e25cf1ae878f2a69c2d1011f6981e4141b39287d44eb4.jpg) caught the imagination, and in the suburbs of Philadelphia German farmhouses were renovated.19By the late 192os speculative builders were producing developments on a significant scale which were centred on specific historical themes. ## Commerce and consumerism in Britain Historians of design have often played down the popular and commercially successful in the interwar years, following the line of contemporary design reformers who have suggested that cheap historicist or modernistic mass-produced items were often purchased as a result of a lack of education in matters of taste.
Yet for the consumer or user their forms and decoration were often laden with meaning and associations, whether or not Pevsner in his Enquiry into Industrial Art of 1937 condemned them as part of the 9o per cent of industrial products that he adjudged to be ‘artistically objectionable', whether or not they were designed by a named designer or simply copied from, or variants on, long-standing precedents.
With the exception of museums such as the Geffrye Museum in London or site museums such as Ironbridge Gorge or Beamish examples of this kind are rarely collected by museums, let alone located in the context ofordinary' rooms.
Such objects are generally seen as artistically deficient rather than culturally significant; documentation concerning their use by consumers is hard to come by; often material concerning their design, production, and distribution has often simply been thrown away.
However, research20 into such areas has been slowly developing, with a steady stream of publications about methodology and possible approaches.21However, highly commercial styles often signify more than the fact that they are ephemeral trends and, in the case of Tudor, Elizabethan, and Jacobean formulae, can be seen to embrace notions of national identity in design, as will be discussed in Chapter 4.
Similarly, the floral patterns adorning countless tea-cups and furnishing textiles may be interpreted as communicators of an essential' Englishness rather than summarily dismissed as hackneyed designs.
The Art Deco style exerted a significant impact in Britain across many design media and was a highly commercial style, including many items at the cheap, novelty end of the market.
Its flat, coloured, geometric patterns could be found in the ‘sunrise' motifs (contemporary symbols of health) on thousands of wooden garden gates, front doors, gable ends, packaging, fabric designs, carpets, tableware, jewellery, and other ornamental products.
Its zig-zag, chevron, and other geometric patterns could also be found in typography, posters, and shop-fronts.
The Deco vocabulary was widely adopted in both interior and exterior designs for cinemas, particularly those associated with Oscar Deutsch's Odeon chain.
Other notable commissions included Ronald Atkinson's 1932 foyer of the Daily Express Building in Fleet Street, London, Oliver Bernard's foyers for the Strand Palace Hotel of 1929-3o and the J.
Lyons and Company Ltd's New Oxford Street Corner House in central London, and Wallis, Gilbert, and Partners' Hoover factory in West London of 1931-2.
There were also a number of potteries producing a wide range of artifacts, including tea and coffee services, bowls, vases, and ornaments at prices which many could afford.
Among the more notable manufacturers were Carlton Ware, Foley Potteries, A.
E.
Gray, and Shelley Potteries [49]; women designers, including Susie Cooper, Clarice Cliff, and Charlotte Rhead, were also prominent in the field. ## Other sites of commercial display: England and France Barometers of commercialproduction and consumer interest in Britain may be found in trade catalogues and periodicals, as well as the range of home-making magazines which grew considerably after the war.
The vast range of exhibits at the annual British Industries Fairs (which commenced on an annual basis in 1915 as a manufacturers' 'shopwindow') and the displays and show houses at the increasingly popular Daily Mail Ideal Home Exhibitions are also revealing.The latter commenced in 1908, with 16o,00o visitors in its first year, and nearly 700,000 even in the depression of the early 193os.
In the 1950s and 196os there were regularly more than I million visitors, tailing off in the later 1970s and early 198os to an average of about 900,000.
Many of the exhibitions were widely reported in the media, and catalogues and related ephemera, including visual material, are extant.22 In France the idea of domestic management caught the public imagination.
Martine Segalen, social anthropologist, sociologist, and historian has described the Salon des Art Ménagers (SAM, Exhibition ## 49 Eric Slater Vogue shape teaset, Shelley Potteries, Longton, 1930 The geometric forms and flat, colourful pattern of this popular teaset reflect the influences of both Cubism and Art Deco.
Slater had been made design director in 1928, and through the introduction of a number of Deco-inspired designs, including Mode, Eve, and Regent in the early 1930s, firmly established Shelley as a popularizer of contemporary French styles. ![](images/6ad6f9961691fd6e48ef0567e7fb475f069200fb74935e3166134c65e0fec224.jpg) of Domestic Science) held as public exhibitions in Paris between 1923 and 1983 as the most vocal institution providing the French popular classes with information, norms, and education on all aspects of housing furnishing, home decoration and domestic management.
As a producer and consumer society developed, in which producers undertook to develop goods geared towards the home, the SAM occupied an instrumental position between those who manufactured domestic goods and those who were expected to buy them.23 It began in the Champde Mars in Paris in 1923 as the ‘Salon des Appareils Ménagers' with a clear focus on domestic appliances, attracting over 1oo,00o visitors, and moved to the Grand Palais in 1926 where it was retitled the ‘Salon des Arts Ménagers'.
In the same year Paulette Bernège founded the Institut d'Organisation Ménagère (Institute for Household Organization) and in 1932 was a key figure in the establishment of the Ligue d'Organisation Ménagère (League for Household Organization).
The prime mover behind the Salons themselves was Jules-Louis Breton, who had been Under-Secretary for State for inventions during the war, and who also coined the termarts ménagers'.
Both Breton and Bernège were important figures in what was essentially an educational movement, one which attracted increasing public interest.(In Britain perhaps the nearest equivalent was the Council for Scientific Management in the Home—COSMITH— which had begun in 1931.) By the 193os the Salons had embraced the exhibition of furniture and room settings, and the work of members of the UAM (Union des Artistes Modernes) was frequently featured.
In 1939 the Salon attracted 6o8,ooo, a figure which rose in the postwar years to more than 1,4oo,ooo in 1955.
However, as patterns of consumption changed and marketing and retailing mechanisms became increasingly sophisticated, the socio-educational role of the Salons was diminished, leading to their final demise as public events in 1983. ![](images/fbfbb5ce048486302c27b0a95c481ad23d0d6375677d95b8109a3bdc400744e1.jpg)
