# Multinational Corporations and Global Products ## The corporate personality: invention and identity From a critical perspective it may be argued that the idea of corporate identity or personality, as articulated by designers and consultancies, is often little more than a contradiction in terms [97, 98]. Some of the ways in which symbols and imagery from the past have been used to validate particular outlooks have been considered in the 1983 collection of essays edited by Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger entitled The Invention ofTradition.¹ Interestingly, at the end of the decade, this book was viewed by Wally Olins, a leading figure in corporate identity design and chairman of the design consultancy Wolff Olins, asfascinating'and ‘brilliant', perhaps acknowledging the relevance of the two key words of the title for those working in his profession.² Furthermore, the power to communicate a very selective portrayal of company activity through a major element in corporate communication, the annual company report,3 was also seen by Olins as a particular kind of invention: In the world of the annual report there are many similarities with Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland. Big things can look small and small things look big. The world is neatly parcelled up into sections that suit a company's organisation. Brazil, for example, disappears with most of South America and all of Africa into a place called Rest of the World'. All the people who work for the corporation have, of course, made major contributions to the business . . . There are no divisions, no splits, no rifts. Everything in the garden is just lovely.⁴ ## Corporate projection and identity creation The corporate identity creation business developed dramatically with the growth of multinational corporations and the emergence of global products such as Coca-Cola, McDonald's hamburgers [99] or the Sony Walkman [100, 101]. It was an aspect of the design profession that became increasingly significant in the post-Second World War period. F.H.K. Henrion, who established Henrion Design Associates (HDA) in 1951, was a pioneer in the field in Britain and, in 1967, defined corporate identity thus:
![](images/c0c8b6adc4f844448f7cbee7e0cfb8ba03e93652efd694249d5edc7fe41784ea.jpg) ![](images/47914a45dd442d849756050ba92d2af630a2081ea841b0ddd2f770b2b5b14e21.jpg) ![](images/f10842b2e329876a74c192ce93cfbab2131f688d207da4a195baa11b62d09acb.jpg) ![](images/b0ecd2325115e6c0ef36c5a8e2ef79b22bfccbc61576cb88a6fd0710a0d57644.jpg) Simms ![](images/c38ad6f65e17e32da592a2fd73ca3fd5b5510549261bcb50c5825e8f3dc9d53d.jpg) ![](images/eaf98fd885c9527416c43eaf53eff4a9c4f9cb4277a45f044647ec38a6b14211.jpg) ![](images/12f6c16f36381f245433986777db2ed7d4b0f6df11a669450b669d701fcf7874.jpg) # LUCAS GEB ## CROSLAND FILTERS ![](images/ef1894df84940f4a18035f7368d590cd7fbe79789a5085cef456e607b56fc657.jpg) ![](images/16fc9037ecfe5c27bab7bcfeaf546bef5e3cf34c4435544e7d54569f576e631c.jpg) G CAV ![](images/a31a023db999df02ce87692cfce874cf3bb9e3f415f344b805c15c3674921b4d.jpg) ## 97 Pre-Pentagram Lucas Identity Programme: Constituent Companies: individuai trade marks and symbols for Lucas subsidiaries before redesign, illustrated in Pentagram, 1970s ## 98 Pentagram Lucas Identity Programme: Constituent Companies (after redesign), 1975 Corporate identity design became an increasingly important aspect of commercial and industrial life in the post-1945 decades. In this instance Lucas Industries called in the Pentagram design consultancy to reassess its corporate projection. In 97 the uncoordinated imagery of Lucas's constituent companies failed to communicate its global significance and size in terms of manufacturing parts for the aerospace, automotive, and industrial sectors. Pentagram proposed the 'Lucas Diagonal' as a solution (98), a diagonal stripe which could be emblazoned on the products, manuals, packaging, transport vehicles, and other visible aspects of company identity. Together with a corporate alphabet and the controlled use of colour, it was felt that this gave all constituent elements a visual coherence and obvious common link which was previously lacking. ![](images/44ece4a50a1d7d27f298888d9f3652ea1d0c22abd4c37bbefca12e7d216a4c54.jpg) A corporation has many points of contact with various groups of people. It has premises, works, products, packaging, stationery, forms, vehicles, publications and uniforms, as well as the usual kind of promotional activities. These things are seen by customers, agents, suppliers, financiers, shareholders, competitors, the press, and the general public, as well as its own staff. The people in these groups build up their idea of the corporation from what they see and experience of it. An image is therefore an intangible and essentially complicated thing, involving the effect of many and varied factors on many and varied people with many and varied interests.⁵ In effect, Henrion was highlighting both the need to promote a clear and coherent image in the quest for corporate success and the abilities and expertise of design consultancies to bring such perceptions effectively into the public arena. However, with the growth of interest in the concept of design management in the 197os and 198os, it was suggested with increasing frequency that corporate identity initiatives should be closely integrated with company infrastructure and policy initiatives. In this evolving climate Wally Olins consistently argued strongly for such a linking of corporate personality with the painstaking analysis of management structures and marketing strategies. Writing in the late 198os, he pronounced: We are entering an epoch in which only those corporations making highly competitive products will survive. This means, in the longer term, that products from major companies around the world will become increasingly similar. Inevitably, this means that the whole of a company's personality, its identity, will become the most significant factor in making a choice between one company and its products and another.6 ## Problems of evaluation Such a positive affirmation by a design consultant of the corporate need for the expression of individual personality in the face of increasinghomogeneity of products indirectly highlights the difficulties inherent in a historical evaluation of the relative economic significance of corporate identity creation in the post-Second World War period. ![](images/4a5b274d863b038152b0045c43d4431875ad2200c4a1a4767361f1364523c42e.jpg) ## 99 Stanley C. Meeston McDonald's at Des Plaines, Illinois, 1955 Hamburgers were first marketed from White Castle restaurant outlets which were launched in Wichita, Kansas in 1921 (see also 34), the decade in which fast-food franchising was launched by Howard Johnson. Other well-known chains included Harland Sanders's Kentucky Fried Chicken, which was prominent by the 1950s. However, it was the readily identifiable corporate symbolism of McDonald's (later including the parabolic arches as part of its logo) which represented the American lifestyle across the world. McDonald's is the world's largest foodservice organization and the leading brand-name in the United States. This is particularly problematic if the weight of evidence is drawn from the design profession itself since, as the twentieth century has unfolded and consumerism blossomed, it has become significantly more important for the growing ranks of design consultants and the burgeoning design press to convince the business and manufacturing sectors that design can play a critical economic role in the market-place. This perceivedneed for a positive portrayal of the effectiveness of corporate identity design has resulted in numerous articles and texts written by those in, or closely connected with, the design profession. The British design historian and theorist Steve Baker, in an extremely useful Olins-focused evaluation of historical approaches to corporate identity design published in 1989, highlighted the problem thus: Olins is an aggressive publicist of his firm's approach to corporate identity; he claimed in 1988 that ‘there's nobody else from Britain apart from us doing it properly'. His writings must, of course, be understood as inseparable from his business activities. In a 1981 article in Designer called'Getting New Business', he suggested that any effective design consultant should ensure that they published articles in ‘influential publications like Management Today or The Director'. He also explained that one of his firm's tactics for attracting a particular company's business was to send its chief executive a copy of TheCorporate Personality.? Furthermore, the design press, which flourished remarkably in the entrepreneurial, service- and distribution-oriented climate of the 198os, has inevitably been dependent on advertising revenue from the design profession and its clients. Unsurprisingly, the majority of articles in this specialized sector of the media have tended towards the reportage of the output or ideology of successful individual designers, design practices, or companies embracingdesign as a visible aspect of their corporate life. However, such examples have provided much of the source material for the many celebratory, design-centred narrative corporate histories which have, in turn, been constructed in comparative isolation from the wider political, economic, social, and cultural complexities of the market-place. Of greater potential value to the historian of twentieth-century design are company, institutional, organizational and individual designer archives, although these too are often problematic as evaluative tools. Much depends on the extent to which the sheer bulk of ## 100 Sony Walkman advertisement, 1980s This advertisement, with its constituent images drawn from several countries, literally shows the global nature of the Walkman, now adopted as a generic name for a product type launched in July 1979. First marketed in the United States as the Soundabout, in Sweden as the Freestyle, and in Britain as the Stowaway, the Walkman has been a phenomenal international success. It demonstrated typical Japanese ingenuity in producing a highly innovative product without a commensurately large investment in new technology. ![](images/6a90a31f29acfa93c8ab713fea169a22a82f984349a476aebfd63a2a12aa2b09.jpg) The idea was simple: Simply create a new Sony Walkman so small it's about the same size as an ordinary cassette case. Sound easy? No, it sounds spectacular. Because even though now it's smaller and lighter, performance has actually been improved. And that took the revolutionary style of thinking Sony is famous for. The super sounding Walkman. The World's Smallest HiFi WALKMAN American Express Credit Card, 1990s The American Express card was first introduced in 1958, following the introduction of the Diners Club card in 1950, which itself stemmed from American corporate credit practices of the 1930s. Since then credit cards have become symbols of affluence and status, instantly recognizable as multinational graphic images and plastic counterparts to global products such as Levi's or Coca-Cola. ![](images/94837ebcaa8f6699c65c3f25ec1397f88f8b40225c9bb71578b7126f137dceff.jpg) material in particular archives has been given over to editing, selection, or even destruction of potentially damaging evidence. Indeed, corporate confidential policies relating to boardroom minutes and sensitive policy decisions have in some cases resultedin the excising from the records of controversial or unfavourable comment. ## Critiques of corporate power and influence Writing from less design-oriented perspectives many other writers8 have presented a different view of the power of the multinational corporation to influence social, economic, and political life. As the American economist J. K. Galbraith argued in his introduction to the 1974 British edition of his widely-read book, The New Industrial State: It is central to my case that power in modern industrial society resides with the large producing organisations—the corporations. So, far from being safely and resignedly subordinate to the market, as the neo-classical argument holds, they fix prices, and go on extensively to accommodate the consumer to their needs. And they also obtain from the state such further action as is needed to ensure a benign and stable environment for their operations.9 This, Galbraith argued, was brought about through the economic power of the large-scale corporation to compete with the state in terms of planning and influence. In 1968, General Motors had a gross revenue of \$22.8 billion, equivalent to about one-eighth of the total receipts of Federal Government in the United States. It accorded with Galbraith's model of large-scale American capitalism in its ability, through sheer size, to influence government, control markets, and dictate prices and wage settlements for the whole automobile industry (only one element of its industrial activities), as well as establishing patterns of consumer taste. Cover of Time magazine showing Coca-Cola as the 'World's Friend', 15 May 1950 This celebrated illustration confirmed the way in which Coca-Cola had become a truly global product by the midcentury, much stimulated by its popularity amongst American troops stationed across the world during the Second World War and its aftermath. It came to be readily associated with the material values and desires of American consumer society, a symbol of material affluence. Such critiques often assumed a more overt political dimension with the global marketing of products which were increasingly identified with a particular way of life. This assumed particular strength in the immediate post-1945 period when products such as Coca-Cola [102] and Levi's jeans became emblems of a ‘democratic', essentially American, lifestyle in countries such as Japan [103] and Germany which were seeking to throw off their recent associations with oppressive political regimes. This process has intensified in the post-Berlin Wall era of the 199os with the proliferation in the former Eastern bloc of McDonald's restaurants andother outlets and products identified with the overt values of consumerism and at least symbolic freedom of choice'. ## 102 Critiques of what has been termed American cultural imperialism' were often highly politicized, as in Ariel Dorfman and Armand ![](images/fc2a5d03770a3f458265658664415b7c67389540d53126f0ff19341ac5ac45fc.jpg) Levi's advertisement, Japan, early 1980s: 'Since 1850 Jeans Have Been Called Levi's in the USA' Although jeans originated in the mid-nineteenth century as Californian workers' clothing made by Levi Strauss they have since become potent and expressive emblems of widely differing values throughout the twentieth century. Associated with teenage rebellion in the 1950s on the one hand, or expensive Designer' brand names in the late 1970s and early 1980s on the other, their changing meanings paralleled those of the T-shirt which successfully made the transition from working vest to emblematic carrier of slogans and images. ![](images/272487bbb66e8914e14d9e7d060abd2a48f6de9ff374bb7627937bf40c028de7.jpg) Mattelart's controversial text of 1971 Para Leer al Pato Donald (How to Read Donald Duck),10which was written in the volatile climate of the Chilean revolution. An ideology associated with the consumerist nirvana of wealth and leisure, as epitomized by the extensive range of American comics, films, and television programmes which sustained such an outlook, was denounced by the authors as irrelevant to the real needs of under-developed countries, particularly Chile, which they saw as having become fundamentally dependent, in economic and cultural terms, on the United States. The highly visible presence internationally of logotypes and branding associated with specific products and companies has been a powerful testimony to the perceived ability of design to communicate particular cultural values, as well as to engender corporate profitability. In a later text Mattelart also drew attention to widespread perceptions that multinational corporations, and their products, were seen increasingly as threats to national sovereignty. However, there was evidence that this was recognized by business itself: . . . in April 1975, the President of the large North American publicity agency Doyle-Dane-Bernbach11asserted before students of a Canadian University that Multinational corporations could solve a part of their image problem through the establishment of global universities'. And, he added, going further into the description of his project, that by adopting this formula companies such as Exxon, Texaco or General Electric would have much less need for support by Government, trades union circles and consumers from accusations made against them of violating national sovereignty. The proposal is very simple: the companies would open a university course of two years for students from both industrialised and underdeveloped countries, with the requirement only that they spoke perfect English'. These courses could deal with the history of the company, the analysis of concrete examples of marketing, management, international law, the relationship of the enterprise with the community, its social responsibility. Provided with a diploma granted by the company, the students would return to their respective countries and would constitutea kind of common denominator of understanding'around the world.12 ## Early manifestations of corporate identity: a historical overview Although corporate identity has assumed an increasingly high profile in the post-1945 era, it has manifested itself over a far longer period through the formation, organization, and visual projection of groups as varied as armies,13 political regimes,14 and railway companies. In Britain, for example, the great railway companies of the nineteenth century made concerted attempts to project their own individual identities across many aspects of their visible presence, from railway termini through to coach livery, uniforms, and dining-car tableware. Design historians have laid particular emphasis on the corporate identity work of designers such as Peter Behrens at the Allgemeine Elektrizitäts-Gesellschaft in the early years of the twentieth century in Germany, as discussed in Chapter 1. Significant examples of corporate identity policies can be found in many other countries, as in Britain in the buildings, locomotives, rolling stock, buses, signage, advertising, fittings, and fabrics of the London Passenger Transport Board under the operationaldirection of Frank Pick in the 193os, or in the United States withWalter Dorwin Teague's striking designs for Texaco petrol stations. Other notable examples prior to the Second World War include the Olivetti office equipment company in Italy, where a corporate identity policy emerged in the wake of Adriano Olivetti's initiatives in modernizing the firm's business and production methods in the later 192os. Much of the impetus had derived from a visit to the United States in 1926, and an advertising office was established in 1928. Following his appointment as general manager in 1933, a wide range of initiatives were adopted in the projection of the public, and also internal, identity of the company, sustained by the employment of a number of leading modernist architects and designers who worked on all aspects of the company's visible appearance, from brochures, advertising andoffice machines through to factory buildings and workers' housing. A Bauhaus graduate, Alexander Schawinsky, workedon graphic and product design from 1933 to 1936; Marcello Nizzoli, a renowned exhibition and graphic designer, became the company's chief consultant in 1936; in the same year Giovanni Pintori also joined the company and, like Nizzoli, added to Olivetti's reputation through publicity, product, and architectural design. This very much set the scene for the further development of an enlightened corporate policy in the post-Second World War era withthe employment of designers of the stature of Ettore Sottsass Jr. and Mario Bellini and the increasingly significant role given to cultural projection. The company's commitment to corporate identity design was recognized in 1974 when the American Institute of Architects awarded Olivetti the Industrial Arts Medal for a history of excellence in communicating its image through product design, corporate communications, architecturally distinguished manufacturing and merchandising facilities, and sponsorship of numerous social, educational, recreational, and cultural programs for both its employees and the public at large'. In the United States corporate identity design also assumed increasing importance in the interwar years. The Container Corporation of America (CCA) was an important pioneer in this respect in the 193os, largely through the enlightened patronage of the company's founder,the Chicago industrialistWalter P. Paepke. In 1936, wishing to communicate the company's commitment to a modern outlook and product quality, he employed the N. W. Ayer advertising agency as a means of bringing this about. In the same year he also appointed Egbert Jacobsen as Director of the company's new Design Department. Amongst those designers commissioned to produce advertisements were the French designers A. M. Cassandre and Fernand Léger, the former Bauhaus tutors Lázló Moholy-Nagy and Herbert Bayer, Herbert Matter, the Swiss emigré designer and poster artist, and the Hungarian-born graphic designer, Gyorgy Kepes. Combinations of photomontage with typography and other techniques associated with the European avant-garde were incorporated into company publicity, strongly influencing the outlook of other designers working for the company. Such strong links with European modernism were sustained by the establishment, in 1937, of the New Bauhaus in Chicago under Lázló Moholy-Nagy. Later becoming the School of Design, then School of Design inChicago, and finally the Institute of Design,15 a number of former Bauhaus graduates and masters were employed on the staff. In the post-Second World War period Walter Paepke, Egbert Jacobsen, and Herbert Bayer were at the forefront of moves which sought to further understanding in business circles of the significant economic potential of design in industry. In 1951 Paepke inaugurated the first Design Conference at the Aspen Institute of Humanistic Studies in Colorado.16Initiating debate about the wider social, cultural, and philosophical implications of design it sought to bring together leading figures from design, industry, government, and education. At the 1951 meetingboth Olivetti and the Container Corporation of America were cited asexemplars of the implementation of a consistent design policy in industry. Held annually, in 1954 it became incorporated as the International Design Conference in Aspen (IDCA) and was soon established as a major forum for design debate, with contributions from leading designers, intellectuals, and industrialists from all over the world. ## Design and the multinational corporation after 1945 As has been discussed in Chapter 4, the aspirations of those seeking to implement the modernist creed in the interwar years had been severely blunted by the rising tide of national identity in the increasingly difficult political and economic circumstances of the times. However, after the Second World War, with the widespread discrediting of totalitarian regimes and the waning of the power of imperialism in the Western industrialized world, the internationalizing values inherent in modernism no longer carried the same threat to national identity. With the postwar reorientation of traditional trading patterns and the need to develop new outlets many large-scale companies viewed the penetration of global markets as an increasingly important goal. As part of this strategy multinational corporations assumed the mantle of modernism, their international presence marked by efficient-looking buildings, products, and co-ordinated corporate design programmes. As has been suggested earlier, the Olivetti company epitomized high standards for corporate identity design and implementation. It was particularly influential on the outlook of International Business Machines (IBM), a company which emerged as a world leader in the field of office equipment after the end of the Second World War. IBM's distinctive corporate style, which embraced everything from brochures and sign systems to dictating machines and company buildings, emerged after the appointment of the architect-designer Eliot Noyes as Consultant Director of Design in 1956 [104]. He had first worked on the IBM account in Norman Bel Geddes's office ten years earlier, continuing to work on a company retainer after setting up his own design practice in 1947. He brought in Paul Rand as Graphics Coordinator as well as a number of other design consultants including Charles Eames, George Nelson, and Edgar Kaufmann Jr. They were all heavily influenced by European modernism: Noyes had worked with the former Bauhaus masters Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer at Harvard in the 193os, and was Director of the Department of Industrial Design at the Museum of Modern Art (MOMA) in New York from 1940-2 and 1945-6; Paul Rand was well aware of European modernism in the interwar years, an interest stimulated by magazines such as the German Gebrauchsgraphik17 and Advertising Arts; George Nelson had studied in Rome in the 193os and, with the designer Henry Wright, co-edited Architectural Forum, a magazine which strongly promoted the modernist cause and frequently featured many aspects of corporate design; after a brief interregnum by Suzanne Wasson-Tucker, Edgar Kaufmann Jr. had succeeded Noyes as Director of the ## 104 Eliot Noyes Selectric typewriter, IBM, 1961 Noyes, who had worked for Gropius and Breuer in the 1930s, had also been director of industrial design at MOMA, New York. He was brought in as design consultant to IBM in 1956 by the corporation's President, Thomas Watson, and soon gave the company a modern, international corporate image. This pervaded its buildings, graphic communications, and products, much in the way that previously the image for the Olivetti company had done. This particular typewriter also introduced the ‘golfball' as a replacement for type-bars. ![](images/affa85c0f8fb2b0dd21580216f17f2ddf27457015422402956d946a3097457f9.jpg) Department of Industrial Design at MOMA, a strong advocate of modernism and promoter of the annual Good Design Exhibitions held at the Museum between 1950 and 1955. Marcel Breuer and Eero Saarinen, an American architect-designer with Scandinavian roots, were also commissioned to design buildings for IBM. The IBM design outlook was enshrined in its Design Practice Manual, written by Noyes. The company soon became renowned for a corporate identity which symbolized advanced technology andorganizational efficiency through its crisp graphics (as in Rand's logotype of 1956, see 105), the neat, clean lines of such office products as the 1961 Selectric typewriter, and the efficient, functional, yet pleasant, ethos of its architecture and interiors. Such an outlook (also promoted by Olivetti and other companies) additionally endowed the office environment with notions of status and aesthetic sensitivity and did much to help persuade potential employees that clerical work was an attractive alternative to the often more lucrative wage potential of competing factory work in the 195os and 196os.18 IBM's policy of design coordination throughout the corporation was continued in the following decades, resulting in official recognition from the American design profession: in 198o IBM was awarded both the Design Leadership Award by the American Institute of Graphic Arts and an award for long-term excellence in design by the Industrial Designers of America (IDSA). Other large American companies were also significant exponents of corporate identity in the decades following the Second World War. By the mid-195os theWestinghouse Electric Corporation had become increasingly concerned with its design image, with frequent complaints by retailers that the company was not oriented clearly enough towards the consumer and could not keep up with its competitors in terms of product development. Its position was further affected by a
# BT 105 Corporate logos: Paul Rand for IBM (1956) and Westinghouse (1960), Henrion Design for KLM (1964), Wolff Olins for BT (1991) Corporate design was an important part of the armoury of national and multinational corporations in the post-Second World War period. These particular symbols and their designers are celebrated in their field. series of strikes and the radical dropping of prices in 1956 by General Electric, the market leader in consumer appliances. Following detailed analysis of the position, Eliot Noyes was brought in to Westinghouse in 196o in order to improve standards. In turn he brought in Paul Rand, who produced a striking logotype, based on electric circuitry and the letter 'W'. Noyes's other consultancies have included Mobil (1964) and Pan-Am (1969-72), whilst Rand has also produced logos for ABC Television and United Parcels Service. The interiors of many large corporations were also endowed with an internationalizing modernist aesthetic, sustained by the furniture of companies such as Herman Miller and Knoll. Although Herman Miller had begun to explore a modernist outlook in the 193os through the enlightened appointmentof Gilbert Rohde as the company's designer, it was not until the appointment of George Nelson as director of design in 1944 that the company began to orient itself towards the architectural, and thus largely corporate, market. Nelson also brought in Charles Eames as a consultant to the company, reinforcing the modernist ethos in furniture production. There was considerable activity in the field of office furniture, most notably the Action Office, which was developed from the late 195os by Nelson and Robert Propst, and marketed in its first version from 1964. Knoll Associates, founded by the German-born Hans Knoll and his wife Florence in New York in 1946, also did much to support the modernist corporate environment through its furniture and furnishings, which could be found in many of the impressive foyers of large corporations [106]. Florence had studied at the Cranbrook Academy of Art and at the Illinois Institute of Technology, both institutions with strong European affiliations. She also knew Mies van der Rohe and worked withGropius and Breuer. Building on such links, the Knolls marketed designs by leading Europeans, many of them being seen as classics' of modern design, especially those by Breuer, Saarinen, and Mies, who granted the company the production rights of his designs of the 192os. Other companies gained considerable recognition for their identity in the same period. In Germany, for example, the Braun company set high standards of a coherent rational design aesthetic with the introduction of Otl Aicher and Hans Gugelot from the pioneering Hochschule für Gestaltung at Ulm alongside the industrial designer, Dieter Rams, in the mid-195os. In 1956 the company's design department was established, coming under Rams's direction in 196o. During his lengthy association with the company a clear identity emerged, characterized by the white, sculptural form of the KM₂ Kitchen Machine designed by G.A. Müller in 1957 [107] or the HLD4 Hairdryer designed by Rams in 197o. The austere, efficient lines of the company's domestic appliances were complemented bythe rational ![](images/0f962a9b5b6cc0b55a171b5a8eebab2ce0c85a438aa5114f46b488c1f295a862.jpg) ## 106 Knoll International furniture showroom, USA, 1950s The styling of the furniture and spatial organization of this interior typifies the international modernism projected by multinational corporations after 1945. This could be seen in the work for Knoll by Eero Saarinen, Harry Bertoia (whose famous lattice steel wire Diamond chair (1952) can be seen in the centre of the floor) and by Florence Knoll herself, whose sideboard can be seen on the extreme left. Hans and Florence Knoll also forged links with other leading American and European designers, producing furniture under licence by Mies and Breuer. The company established a reputation for Good Design much in line with the aesthetic principles espoused by Kaufmann at MOMA, New York. spirit underlying its corporate graphics, advertising, and packaging. It should be considered, in passing, that a coherent design programme did not in itself ensure market success: American Gillette took Braun over, andfurther difficulties were experienced in the competitive market-place of the early 199os. The work of a wide range of influential corporate identity consultancies such as Chermayeff & Geismar Inc. of New York, Pentagram of London or Total Design of Holland might be enumerated in this context, along with many instances of a multinational corporate design policy, such as those adopted by Philips,19 Coca-Cola,20or Sony.21 However, there are other mechanisms worthy of attention which have done much to support the globalization of specific products or cultural values, many of them enshrined in the corporate ethos of companies already discussed. ## The role of museums and exhibitions in promoting a global sesign culture While a growing number of museums are beginning to embrace wider definitions of design culture in the twentieth century, the majority have endorsed a policy which is centred on celebrated products or the output of specific designers whose work is seen to embrace high standards of aesthetic distinction or cultural status.The twentieth-century design galleries of many museums around the world have their roots in the collection and display of objects which, it was originally felt, would improve' standards of taste and enhance the cultural well-being of their visitors. Furthermore, those charged with selection policies and the acquisition of material were generally drawn from a narrow social and cultural spectrum and, when they were bold enough to step outside their own national conventions of artistic excellence, oftenfavoured objects which conformed to the modernist canon. The meanings of such clean, abstract forms, stripped of superfluous ornamentation and symbolically compatible with the modern machine-age production technology, have changedalongside the reshapingof culturaland political perspectives both before and after the Second World War, as has been discussed in Chapter 2 (and will be examined further in Chapter 8). As has been argued, modernist products became increasingly associated with notions ofGood Design', opposed both to retrospective indulgence in historicizing ornament in domestic products on the one hand and to the science-fiction-inspired futuristic chrome fantasies and tail-fins of automobiles on the other. Modernist products were also seen as oppositional to notions of built-in obsolescence and ephemerality and thus, particularly when placed in a spotlit, pedestalized museum—rather than a social—context, assumed something of the status ofdesign classic'. ## Modernism and MOMA, New York MOMA, founded in New York in 1929 to encourage and develop the study of the modern arts and the application of such arts to manufacture and public life', did much to establish such an outlook. Its Department of Architecture and Industrial Art was established in 1932 ## 107 Gerd Alfred Muller and Robert Oberheim Kitchen Machine KM 32, Braun, 1957 By the mid-1950s Braun emerged as a company with high aesthetic principles in product design, having forged links with the nationalist Hochschule für Gestaltung at Ulm. A design department was established at the company in 1956, the KM3 of the following year epitomizing the geometric clarity which was to be associated with Braun products for many years, particularly after 1960 when Dieter Rams became Braun's chief designer. A permanent display of Braun products was put on display at MOMA, New York, in 1958. ![](images/5aa01b42c08c04fd561bd31b474f75a37acc7286d056ca2ce12ef1f9bd489d06.jpg) and mounted a series of didactic design exhibitions promoting modernism, commencing with the Machine Art show of 1934 which was curated by Philip Johnston. It was in the same year that MOMA's Design Collection was formally inaugurated, commencing with a selection from the Machine Art exhibition [12]. Two criteria were identified for the selection of objects—quality'and 'historical' significance: An object is chosen for its quality because it is thought to achieve, or have originated, those formal ideals of beauty which have become the major style concepts of our time. Historical significance is a more flexible criterion. It applies to objects which may not resolve problems of aesthetics and function with total success, but which nevertheless have contributed importantly—or may yet contribute—to the development of design.22 In 1939 the Museum held a ten-year retrospective exhibition in which industrial design played a comparatively minor role. MOMA's stance against the ephemeral styling of American products was revealed by the inclusion of only one American designer, Richard Buckminster Fuller, a fierce critic of contemporary American industrial design. The more favoured European and Scandinavian modernism was represented through chairs by Breuer, Mies Van Der Rohe, Le Corbusier, and Alvar Aalto. This design creed was continued by Eliot Noyes and Edgar Kaufmann Jr., in charge of MOMA's Department of Industrial Design in the 194os and 195os. Kaufmann also mounted a series of Good Design exhibitions between 1950 and 1955 [108, cf. 109], the precepts for which were largely enumerated in his definitive text, What Is ## 108 'Good Design Show'organized by Edgar Kaufmann Jr. for MOMA, NY, 1951 Kaufmann's'Good Design' programme was underpinned by a collaboration between MOMA, New York, and The Merchandise Mart, Chicago, representing respectively the interests of art and commerce. It was aimed at museum audiences and the wholesale buyers who represented the retail trade, seeking to educate both the public and manufacturing industry. The pronounced emphasis on form rather than decoration seen in this installation by Finn Juhl reflected themodernist credo followed by Kaufmann. ![](images/8b343bde6e28ec5eb6a1c9c4ea60b94846a5f63892104d700fc84b898c4774a6.jpg) ![](images/6cb09784b48b55ffedf767aa6719c25584c342a68234eb38765b9f6d7b9ae84d.jpg) ## 109 Frank Gehry Interior of the Vitra Design Museum at Weil am Rhein, 1989 This innovative museum was built largely as a gallery for the chair collection of Rolf Fehlbaum of the Vitra furniture manufacturing company. Pictured here are a number of classic designs including Charlotte Perrier and Le Corbusier's Chaise Longue (1929), Breuer's B3 Wassily chair(1925), Jacobsen's Ant chair (1953), and Eames's lounge chair (1958). Pedestalized and removed from their primary function, they are to be viewed as art and symbols of aesthetic status. ModernDesign?of195o.23Consolidatingsuch a morally-charged approach to design, the exhibition Olivetti: Design in Industry' was put on in 1952, the first time a European manufacturer had been invited to display its products and graphic design at the Museum. Coming two years after the establishment of the Olivetti Corporation of America in New York, the show exemplified what was felt to be good practice, a practice which the companyhad itself done much to validate through external promotion. As was written at the time in MOMA's Bulletin, The Olivetti company, many critics agree, is the leading corporation in the western world in the field of design. For patronage in architecture, product design and advertising, it would only be difficult to name a second . ., It is not only the aesthetic quality of these achievements that is remarkable. More important as a lesson in our industrial world of today is the organisation of all the visual aspects of an industry, unified under a single high standard of taste.24 The postwar inheritance of a form of European modernism was further consolidated when Braun products were put onpermanent display at MOMA from 1958, following growing approbation of the German company's new design policy at the 1957Milan Triennale, the Frankfurt Radio and Television Exposition, and the Berlin
# GREYHOUND SCENICRUISER ![](images/6f1895703150b4d6d985641aa0ea90adc7e8f56deb409807bf5912545a298f85.jpg) 110 Publicity for Scenicruiser Greyhound bus, designed by Raymond Loewy Associates, 1954 Loewy devoted considerable attention to new transportation designs, endowing them with style and panache. He had worked with the Greyhound company since 1940, when he designed the Silversides motor coach. It was replaced by the sleek, streamlined, and obviously American Scenicruiser, and its high standards of passenger comfort, together with the development of the US highway system, were intended to attract inter-city travellers in the face of competition from rail and the air. International Building Exhibition, where its products were seen in the majority of show houses. There was a similar institutionalizationof the notion of Good Design in Europe, often with support from the State, as with the Council of Industrial Design (COID), established in Britain in 1944 or the Rat für Formgebung (Design Council) in Germany, which, following a 1951 mandate in the German Parliament, was inaugurated in 1953. The COID was charged from the outset with ‘improving' standards of design in the consumer and manufacturing sectors and initiated a Good Design Award Scheme for selected products in 1957, the year after opening its own Design Centre in the Haymarket, London. The awardsgenerally recognized products which conformed to the modernist canon—-genteel and restrained, and devoid of excessive ornamentation or ephemeral styling. Similar awards reflecting parallel aesthetic priorities were offered in other European countries, including the Compasso d'Oro scheme, initiated by La Rinascente department store in Italy in 1954, and the Beauté France award, made through the French Ministry of Commerce. That there was an established international canon of taste' in the 1950s can be argued further through the evidence collected by Jay Doblin, Director of the Institute of Design at the Illinois Institute of Technology, in 1958.25 He wrote to 10o of the leading' designers, architects, and design teachers around the world, asking them to identify the ten 'best designed mass-produced products of modern times'. About 8o ballots were returned and, after the issue of further questionnaires, a final order was drawn up. Although the overall ranking was significantly more accommodating with regard to ephemeral styling than would have been the case with MOMA, theCOID, and comparable organizations with a commitment to the concept of Good Design, the top three products were the Olivetti Lettera 22 portable typewriter of 195o, designed by Marcello Nizzoli, the Eames side-chair of 1947, produced by Herman Miller, and Mies Van Der Rohe's Barcelona Chair, originally designed in 1929, produced by Knoll Associates. Raymond Loewy Associates-designed products were featured six times (including the Coldspot refrigerator for Sears Roebuck, a 1948 vacuum cleaner for Singer, and the 1954Scenicruiser greyhound bus [110]), but overall the favoured products generally looked to modernism, with a particular leaning towards designs from Europe and Scandinavia, including designs by Aalto, Barnack, Breuer, D'Ascanio, Ghia, Gretsch, Nizzoli, Pinin Farina, Ponti, Porsche, Thonet Brothers, and Wegner. ## The corporation and cultural heritage As has been seen in the case of Herman Miller and Knoll International in the UnitedStates, a significant number of companies were active in the promotion of the international style through the marketing of high-quality furniture with a heavy premium on aesthetic distinction. Cassina, the Milan-based furniture company, played a similar role, movinginto the field of architect-designed furniture from the late 194os onwards, with a particular emphasis on Italian designers, such as Franco Albini, Gio Ponti, Vico Magistretti, and Mario Bellini. From 1965 it also initiated a policy of producing a range of past classics from the late nineteenth and earlier twentieth centuries. Entitled the Masters'series, it commenced with manufacture, to the original design, of the 1929 chaise longue by Le Corbusier, Charlotte Perriand, and Pierre Jeanneret. Later, particularly in the heritage-aware 198os when thepervasive fashionabilityof Post-Modernism cast many aspects of modernist design into a historical perspective, the Masters' range included the resurrection of furniture by Gunnar Asplund, Breuer, Frank Lloyd Wright, Gerrit Rietveld, and CharlesRennie Mackintosh. Also important in the wider projection of companies has been their involvement in cultural activities, a sphere in which Olivetti has been particularly prominent. Exhibitions specifically centred upon the company's own products and designers were widely disseminated, typified by such shows as Olivetti: Form and Concept put on at the Musée des Arts Decoratifs in Paris (as well as at venues in Barcelona, Madrid, Edinburgh, London, and Tokyo between 1969 and 1971) and Os Artistas e a Olivetti (The Artists and Olivetti) shown in Sao Paolo, Brazil in 1976. However, wider aspects of Italian artistic heritage were celebrated in a series of art-historical films by Carlo Ludovico Ragghianti in the 195os, as well as in exhibitions such as the Italian Modern Art Exhibition 191o-35, drawn from the Mattioli Collection, which was shown in New York and Europe in the late 196os and early 197os. Film andphotography have also been a potentvehicle for the projection of company ethos, environment, design practice, and social policy, with commissions from, and about, other countries, cultures, ecology, and the environment. Even gifts, souvenirs, desk diaries, and company calendars, first introduced in 1951, were a part of the process of establishing the company's personality as cultural. Corporate gifts and souvenirs have included melamine paper knives by Marcello Nizzoli (196o), a melamine desk tidy by Bruno Munari (196o), a canvas brief case by Giorgio Soavi (1965), and an enamelled-iron pencil tray (1966) and electric table clock (1968) by EttoreSottsass Jr., many of which became extremely sought after as status symbols by business executives and managers. ## 'The New International Style' Globalization of the designed object accelerated significantly in the 198os with the emergence of design groups such as Memphis. It originated in 1981 in Milan and, centred around Ettore Sottsass Jr., effectively set on a commercial footingmany ideas which hadoriginated in the studio-based experimentation of 197os Italy. Memphis furniture, lighting, ceramic, glass, and jewellery designs drew upon the symbols, forms, materials, and decorative motifs of mass culture; it utilized seemingly mundane materials such as plastic laminates, and emphasized surface decoration, colour, and layers of meaning at the expense of apparent function. Such products radically undermined both the architectonic principles of the modernist aesthetic inherent in international style furniture and the linear gracefulness that had generally characterized design-conscious Italian products since the Second World War. In addition to Sottsass, the group had a strong international range of contributors to its output, including Andrea Branzi, Michele De Lucchi, Matheo Thun, and Marco Zanini from Italy, Michael Graves and Peter Shire from the United States, Hans Hollein from Austria, Xavier Mariscal from Spain, and Shiro Kuramata and Arata Isozaki from Japan. During the 198os, shows of the group's work were held in the major museums in many capital cities around the world and its products marketed under the banner of the New International Style'.26This notion of a New International Style' indi- ## 111 Philippe Starck Toothbrush for L'Oréal/Goupil Laboratories, France, 1990 With greater emphasis on health, fitness, and hygiene in the 1970s, the bathrooms of the wealthier sectors of society were increasingly characterized as places for leisure and relaxation rather than functional necessity. During the 1980s many associated'designer' products were introduced to this sphere of domestic life. The Starck toothbrush, with its Brancusi-like sculptural form and conical 'pedestal' has become an icon of an emergent'designer' culture. ![](images/7f184781cf3ca1c742e7ab2a3860068f5b71df32b82126884b25b17a0cb5ec05.jpg) cated the commodification of particular cultural concepts within a global context. Endowed with the immediate cultural status conferred through featuring widely in exhibitions and the more image-oriented media across the world, Memphis products were the preserve of an affluent élite who saw them essentially as works of art. This notion of'design as art', where design was generally collected for its visual identity and implicit cultural values rather than any premium on function or practicality [111], was also reinforced by the outlook of companies such as Officina Alessi²7 from Italy or the New York-based Swid Powell [112]. Specializing in what has been termed 'the· tabletop industry'’or micro-architecture',28both companies focused on the commissioning of small-scale pieces of decorative art by well-known architects anddesigners, whose buildings, interiors, tastes, personalities, and exhibitions were increasingly widely covered in the media. Officina Alessi launched a series of Tea and Coffee Piazzas29 which were commissioned from eleven internationally recognizedarchitects [113], including Robert Venturi, Michael Graves, and Charles Jencks from the United States, Alessandro Mendini and Paolo Portoghesi from Italy, Oscar Tusquets from Spain, and Hans Hollein from Austria. The eleven sets were each produced in limited editions of 99, priced individually at about £12,ooo, and galleries in Milan and New York simultaneously hosted their launch in 1983, reinforcing the cultural status and economic exclusivity of the objects. Swid Powell was founded in 1982 by Nan Swid and Addie Powell, significantly both previous employees of Knoll International, the former as design director in product design development, the latter a sales vice-president. Swid Powell's first range of architect-designed pieces, including porcelain dinnerware, glassware, and silverplate, was launched in 1984 in six American cities, proving an instant commercial success in the upper echelons of the market-place. The company continued to maintain a fashionable aura throughout the decade, sustained by such high-profile events as the striking window displays in the Bergdorf Goodman department store which were planned to coincide with the American Institute of Architects'1988 convention in New York. Many of the displays incorporated Swid Powell artefacts, ## 112 Robert Venturi Village, 4-piece tea and coffee set, Swid Powell, 1986 Drawing on an eclectic range of references—historic, high art, and the everyday—this tea set for the highly fashionable Swid Powell company reflected Venturi's Post-Modernist inclinations. The teapot decoration and domed lid with oculus refers to the Pantheon in Rome; the coffee pot derives from the form of a Tuscan tower, the milk jug from a Renaissance palazzo and the sugar bowl from a peasant's cottage. ![](images/30799fe988c9b81c9417321502d2001e0ec8ecd9033b911d4fba0f5b423baf5b.jpg) 162 MULTINATIONAL CORPORATIONS AND GLOBAL PRODUCTS ## 113 Kazumasa Yamashita 5-piece tea and coffee set, Tea and Coffee Piazza series, Alessi, 1983 This coffee set was one of eleven limited editions of the scheme marketed by Officina Alessi and the two venues from which they were launched—the Brera Gallery, Milan, and the Max Protech Gallery, New York—mark out the company's cultural and artistic intentions. Commissioned from high profile designers and architects, these objects of high fashion, destined for museums or the coffee tables of the very wealthy, signified the global nature of 1980s design culture. ![](images/44ed632afdb48a5307ed9064bb91cbfc6988eeffa6a5225c15391290cae9aa19.jpg) their fashionability and status considerably enhanced by the featuring of a number of Swid Powell-commissioned architect-designers alongside celebrated fashion designers. These pairings included Michael Graves and Giorgio Armani, Robert Venturi and Christian Lacroix, and Richard Meier and Calvin Klein. This international dimension was reinforced by the commissioning by Swid Powell of other highprofile designers including Ettore Sottsass Jr., Paolo Portoghesi, Vittorio Gregotti, and the British-born George Sowden from Italy, the Austrian Hans Hollein, and Arata Isozaki from Japan. The metaphorical distance from the tabletops of an affluent international design-conscious clientèle to cultural re-affirmation in the displays of leading museums such as MOMA and the Metropolitan Museum in New York, the Museum Boysmans-van Beuningen in Rotterdam, or the Design Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum in London was small. It is also clear when reviewing the names of many of the designers working for Memphis, Officina Alessi, and Swid Powell and other such enterprises that they and their designs have become global commodities just as have the more anonymous products of IBM, Philips, Sony, or Benetton. ![](images/9765d7430d6ce8736391a1eb5c646f4f276ce4a69f4862b52687d277dab7974f.jpg)
