# Pop to Post-Modernism: Changing Values With a discernible shift of emphasis from production towards consumption¹ in the changing market conditions of the postwar period, questions were raised whether either the monolithic Fordist model, which had hitherto dominated approaches to manufacture for the mass market for much of the twentieth century, or the modernist aesthetic could cater adequately for the increasingly variegated tastes and desires of the consumer [120, 121, 122]. In this connection a number of critics, theorists, and designers became interested in the relationship between visual and linguistic ‘signs', the correlation between the two being embraced in what hasbeen termed semiotics. Writers such as the French sociologist Raymond Barthes, in his seminal text Mythologies of 1957,2 the Italian theorist, critic, and design historian Gillo Dorfles, in Il disegno industriale e la sua estetica3 (Industrial Design and Its Aesthetic) of 1963, and the American Robert Venturi, in Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture⁴ of 1966 did much to open up debates about the perceived shortcomings of the modernist aesthetic. ## Theoretical and critical reorientation In the early 195os Reyner Banham began working on his doctoral thesis, later published as Theory and Design in the First Machine Age.5 It is an important text for design historians as it marks a very different approach to modernism from that of his doctoral supervisor, Nikolaus Pevsner, in his Pioneers of the Modern Movement.6 Representing a shift in critical and theoreticalcircles, particularly that centred on the Independent Group in London, with which Banham was closely associated, it was written at a time when modernist architecture, design, and theory began to be challenged by those who felt that the new postwar era was one which should embrace mass culture and advanced technology. An era of passenger jet transportation, growing affluence and consumer aspirations, expendability and obsolescence, the 195os was also, according to Banham, the Second Machine Age, the age of domestic electronics and synthetic chemicals'.8He also clearly differentiated it from the First Machine Age, the era of modernism: ![](images/1be45a7a5dd5f18458977a147a8ed62ea78427acfd1af885e5ead407a5542922.jpg) ## 120 Toshiyuki Kita Wink Chair, Cassina, 1980 This colourful and versatile seating can be transformed from armchair to chaise longue by tilting the base forward, whilst the back rest can be adjusted by the knobs at its base. The headrests can also be independently adjusted. Like many Post-Modern products it draws upon a range of sources, whether the ethos of Pop through the brightly coloured covers (which can be pulled over the frame like a T-shirt), 'Mickey Mouse' ear-like forms of the headrests, or the automobile world of adjustable seats and headrests. [in] the Second, highly developed mass production methods have distributed electronic devices and synthetic chemicals broadcast over a large part of society—television, the symbolic machine of the Second Machine Age, has become a means of mass-communication dispensing popular entertainment. In the First, however, only cinema was available to a broad public, whose home life was otherwise barely touched and it was in the upper middle-class homes that the First Machine Age made its greatest impact, the homes that could afford these new, convenient and expensive aids to gracious living, the homes that tend to breed architects, painters, poets, journalists, the creators of the myths and symbols by which a culture recognises itself.9 In the early 195os, in the first phase of meetings of what became known as the Independent Group, considerable interest was expressed in science, technology, and the history of design, an emphasis which underlay Banham's firm belief in the liberating force of technology and his stress in Theory and Design on Futurism, which he saw as a turning point in theories of design'(unlike his doctoral supervisor, Pevsner, who considerablydownplayed its significance in Pioneers). At the 1954-5 meetings of the Group—which included Peter and Mary Banham, Lawrence Alloway, Eduardo Paolozzi, Richard and Terry Hamilton, JohnMcHale, Nigel Henderson, and Toni del Renzio— there was considerable interest in popular culture, advertising, and the media in the United States, exemplified in talks such as Banham's Borax or the Thousand Horse-Power Mink' of 1955, which considered the extravagant styling, sensuous advertising, and sexual symbolism of the Americanautomobile. Technologically-inspirediconography influenced the styling of many other appliances as well as the seductive language which helpedto advertise them, as recounted by John McHale in a special Americana issue of the Royal College of Art magazine, Ark in 1956. References to ‘aquamatic action', ‘jet spray', centrifugal clutch drive' in the washing machine, figure well in General Electric's new cooking range names—the Stratoliner and the Liberator. A quote like New Extra Hi-Speed Giant 2,6oo Calrod Unit is 2o per cent faster than gas—by actual test' is straight out of '56 auto ad-speak, and with push-button control,a flick of your finger selects your cooking heat' as well as your gearchange. Automatic cutoffs', 'oventimers', 'circuit-breakers', 'washer and sediment swirl-out' signalled the general preoccupation with robotics, and the 'WondR dial automatically pre-selects' everything from defrosting to the year's breakfasts.10 Twelve members of the IG were involved with the This is Tomorrow exhibition held at the Whitechapel Gallery in London in 1956. Many art historians, encouraged by particular reinterpretations by Banham and Alloway,11 have seen this show as the genesis of Pop Art. They have placed particular emphasis on the environment created by John McHale, John Voelker, and Richard Hamilton, which included an American jukebox playing pop music, a publicity blow-up of Robbie the Robot from the film The Forbidden Planet, and a cut-out of Marilyn Monroe from The Seven Year Itch. However, Anne Massey has convincingly underlined the importance of design as the overarching con- ## 121 James Dyson G-Force Cyclonic Vacuum Cleanermanufactured by Apex Inc., Tokyo, 1986 Designed in 1979, the striking colours of this sculptural, hightech design mark it out as more than a functional object. Rather as the styling of food mixers in the 1950s (see 107) increasingly demarcated them as objects to be displayed on kitchen work surfaces rather than stored in cupboards, so this product endowed the mundaneity of housework with associations of designer-chic in the iconconscious 1980s. Unlike the kitchen appliance seen in 107, this design is redolent with imagery and associations. ![](images/03387985ab83d5d6f1e22548d8e25c28a3e068210b3496faf168ada3351a9d17.jpg) cept'12 of the exhibition. This Is Tomorrow was visited by more than 19,ooo, was widely reported inthe media, and thus brought some of these design-centred ideas before a wider audience. That the potential liberating power of technology was not restricted to theoretical discussions amongst an educated artistic coterie, the interests of the art gallery-going public, or the prurient focus of the media was exemplified in Alison and Peter Smithson's design for a House of the Future'[123] which was shown at the Daily Mail Ideal Home Exhibition in Olympia, London, in 1956. During the mid-1950s these annual exhibitions were regularly visited by more than i million visitors. In 1956 in the Smithsons' vision of the early 198os they could see a wide range of futuristic appliances and equipment, including remote-controlled radio-television and controls for raising sections of the floor for coffee or dining tables in the living room; an eye-level refrigerator, two eye-level ovens, one of which was microwave, and a dishwasher. Another London-based group which embraced notions of expendability, obsolescence, and change as a sign of a vibrant, healthy society was Archigram which received its first public exposure at an exhibition at the Institute of the Contemporary Arts in 1963. Members of the group, disillusioned by the restrictive nature of contemporary architectural practice in Britain, looked to the world of science fiction for a prophetic insight into the future and, like Banham, placed their faith in ## 122 Richard Sapper Kettle with bronze whistle, Alessi, 1983 Like the vacuum cleaner seen in 121, this kettle became a cult icon in fashionable circles in the 1980s. Considerable attention was paid to design for the status-conscious kitchen, with products being made from high-quality materials. Sapper worked on several products for Alessi, including an extensive range of pans and kitchen utensils which was developed in conjunction with leading French and Italian chefs. It was manufactured in 1986 under the name La Cintura di Orione. ![](images/51010d45204bc803f55f3d15da65ef07698fba4a50b4df7fa991e92369ecd0c6.jpg) ## 123 Alison and Peter Smithson 'House of the Future', Ideal Home Exhibition, London, 1956 The Smithsons' design was a projection of automated living in the early 1980s, intended to be mass-produced like automobiles, furnished with an extensive range of built-in equipment and appliances of all kinds. The envisaged technological support for future living was of a high order, even including a portable electrostatic dustcollector which could be set to work on its own anywhere in the house. Such ideas which embraced expendability, obselescence, and change were increasingly attractive to a population which for many years had been restricted to rationing. ![](images/8b438a69487c21ad09cc59732ea89e47d2852ecdc41f8e0171a2be5cc5936d99.jpg) the latest technology—the space capsule, the rocket, the bathyscope, and the handypack. They rejected traditional forms of building and very much looked to a form of architecture which was determined by consumer need. Flexibility, individual choice, and an affinity with popular culture underlay manyof their Utopian schemes such as the Walking City of 1964 and the Instant City of 1968. In Establishment circles there was a clear difference of opinion about what was an appropriate form for modern design. American arbiters of taste, such as Edgar Kaufmann Jr. of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, had placed a very different interpretation of definitions of the requirements that modern design should fulfil from those in the Independent Group or Archigram in Britain. Kaufmann, who had warned British architects and designers about what he saw as the moral dangers of streamlining and styling for the sake of change in his celebrated 1948 article on Borax, or the Chromium-Plated Calf',13 opined that modern design is the planning and making of objects suited to our way of life, our abilities, our ideals', that it should express the spirit of our times', and that it should ‘serve as wide a public as possible, considering modest needs and limited costs no less challenging than the requirements of pomp and luxury'.14 Clearly notions such as our way of life' or our ideals' epitomized a particular social and cultural sector of society. At the Council of Industrial Design (COID) there was a similar resistance to American ideas of built-in obsolescence, ‘style follows sales', and the lure of gadgetry, with a number of admonitory articles in the organization's magazine, Design. Richard Hamilton, painter and member of the Independent Group, was also a significant writer on design and, when he wrote about American practice in a 196o Design article entitled Persuading Image',15 John E. Blake wrote an accompanying editorial, 'Consumers in Danger',16 in which he likened what ![](images/9e4e32624cdf5ed94845c10f53de1781ed54592e352a57314eb15d01306bbae8.jpg) John Stephen attending the opening of Carnaby House in Via Margutti, Rome, 1967 John Stephen had opened his first shop in Carnaby Street in 1957, and in succeeding years did much to enliven men's fashion, drawing on Italian styling. By the mid-1960s he owned several shops in Carnaby Street which by then was at the centre of so-called 'Swinging London'. He opened a number of shops elsewhere in Britain and the USA, as well as twenty-one in Europe of which Carnaby House was one. This photograph shows John Stephen attending the opening in May 1967, accompanied by a typically mini-skirted companion with the almost inevitable Vespa motor scooter parked alongside. he saw as the manipulative techniques of American industry toa form of economic totalitarianism not dissimilar from Orwell's terrifying prophecy'. There are many other layers of what has been termed the Spectre of Americanisation' which have been recounted by writers such as Dick Hebdige in ‘Towards a Cartography ofTaste, 1935-1962'17 andwhich include concerns about the homogenizing effects of pervasive American culture, much like those expressed by many writers in the United States in the 192os. In Britain the writer Richard Hoggart, in his constantly-reprinted text The Uses of Literacy of 1957, examined three facets of this phenomenon in a chapter entitled‘The Newer Mass Art: Sex in Shiny Packets'. He referred to the British Juke-Box Boys' with an ‘American slouch', listening to American tunes on the 'nickelodeon'inmilk-bars': The young men waggle one shoulder or stare, as desperately as Humphrey Bogart, across the tubular chairs.18 Compared even with the pub around the corner, this is all a peculiarly thin and pallid form of dissipation, a sort of spiritual dry-rot amid the odour of boiled milk. Many of the customers—their clothes, their hair-styles, their facial expressions all indicate—are living to a large extent in a myth world compoundedof a few simple elements which they take to be those of American way of life.19 None the less, other social, cultural, and aesthetic shifts were taking place in Britain in the late 195os and 196os which, although embracing many aspects of American-inspired consumer culture, also took on particular dimensions of Italian style, particularly in those sectors of the market-place catering for the young. ## Pop culture in Britain Much has been made by design historians20 of the growth of youth culture and the potential economic significance of the teenage consumer from the late 195os evidenced by Mark Abrams's two-part market research study for the London Press Exchange, The Teenage Consumer,21of 1959-6o. A number of designers and manufacturers responded to the values embraced in the increasing acceptance of change and expendability as a way of life in this emergent market sector. Fashion designers such as Mary Quant and John Stephen [124] who had established their business in the 195os became media-worthy figures in the Pop era of the 196os, when an ever-increasing range of boutiques catered for the rapidly changing lifestyles of a throwaway society'. Bright colours and boldly patterned motifs covered the surfaces of shirts, shopfronts, and shopping bags, as well as everyday domestic items such as coffee mugs. Shirley Craven at Hull Traders Ltd. of Lancashire reflected such trends in her textiles of the 196os; Hull Traders also marketed Bernard Holdaway's 1966 range of cheap, expendable, brightly coloured, simply shaped Tomotom furniture, the epitome of Pop. ![](images/ca0cb5913be223703d89859af892edb9a08236b4d6f70392f9840644db32a2e2.jpg) In a number of design-historical accounts22of British Pop there has been a tendency to position the vibrant, youthful market-place of the 196os alongside the aesthetic predilections of the Council of Industrial Design in order to demonstrate the increasing ideological gulf between the two. The position is sustained by reference to the COID director Paul Reilly's 1967 article on ‘The Challenge of Pop'³ in which the modernist-inspired aesthetic tenets of this organization may be seen to be about to be modified in the light of external change. It has also been suggested that the COID was faced with the dilemma either of accepting the implications of Pop or, through their rejection, of undermining those values that the organization had promoted since its inception. Whilst this is largely self-evident²⁴ it is also clear that, for the everyday consumer, the policies of the COID were completely unknown and irrelevant. However, like MOMA, being an organization that was seen to represent aparticular, and increasingly outmoded, ideological stance, its modernist outlook provided a useful target for those design theorists, writers, and practitioners who were associated with the formulation of the concept of Post-Modernism. ## Cultural pluralism and the mass media ## 125 Vivienne Westwood Savages collection, 1981 A highly influential fashion designer over more than twenty years, Westwood was an important force in the reestablishment of London as a major fashion centre, drawing on a wide range of influences, from the ethnic—as seen here—to historic reinterpretation and street-style. As has been indicated in earlier discussion of the Independent Group and Archigram in Britain, for many professionals involved in the fields of design and architecture the seemingly restrictive vocabulary of the modernist aesthetic was felt to offer an impoverished means of expression in an age when the mass media were able to introduce images and cultures, past and present, from all over the globe at virtually the touch of a button. Such visual encyclopaedismprovided designers and consumers with a rich visual syntax upon which to draw, bringing about a greater sense of freedom to express, through clothes, furniture, or even housing itself, affinities with particular ways of living, or lifestyles' as the market-oriented entrepreneurs of the 197os and 198os were to define it. The fashion designer Vivienne Westwood epitomized the ways in whichdesigners could move, almost effortlessly, through a wide range of stylistic vocabularies in a comparatively short span of time: Punk was promoted through her London shop Seditionaries in the 197os; in 1981 she launched both her Pirates Collection, plundering' the styles and images conjured up by the age of buccaneering, and the Savage Collection [125], with its references to a range of ethnic cultures; the following year saw her Buffalo Collection, which drew on American folk culture for inspiration, the same year in which she launched her London SW1 Nostalgia of Mud Shop, which drew upon Africa; her work has continued to draw upon a diversity of forms of inspiration. ## The genesis of Post-Modernism As indicated at the outset of this chapter, the designer-architect Robert Venturi was an important theorist for what was later to become known as Post-Modernism, and in Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture, published in 1966 (though written in 1962),he made what has subsequently become a widely useddefinition of many of itscharacteristics: elements which are hybrid rather than pure', compromising rather than clear', distorted rather than‘straightforward', ambiguous rather thanarticulated', perverse as well as impersonal', conventional rather than ‘designed', accommodating rather thanexcluding', redundant rather than simple, vestigial as wellas innovating, inconsistent and equivocal rather than direct and clear.25 Architecture and planning were fields which attracted considerable critical attention at the time since, for many writers and consumers, they most vividly exemplified the ways in which the modernist vision had failed those for whom it was intended to provide a better living and working environment.26 Thus, although there have been a number of debates about the exact origins of the term Post-Modernism' in the fields of design andarchitectureit is not surprising that it should appear in the title of an architectural text, Charles Jencks's book The Language of Post-Modern Architecture,27 published in 1977. It came to be seen as a term which usefully embraced those characteristics—such as eclecticism, ornamentation, kitsch, wit, and irony—which most typified the diversity of contemporary culture in a pluralist society. ## The Italian avant-garde: creativity in the face of industrialized capitalism In the increasingly contested debates at the Milan Triennali of the 195os and 196os, manymembers of the Italian avant-garde reacted strongly against notions of 'Italian Style'as the bedrock of Italian design, despite the cultural approbation that the Linea Italiana' or Bel Disegno' had gained in Europe and the United States. They saw the stylized elegance of the furniture, domestic artifacts, and dress of fashionable society, or the design-as-art collections of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, as manifestations of a capitalist society in which the manufacturer was responding to the economic dictates of the market-place rather than the imaginative and creative possibilities of design as a means of enhancing the quality of life. As a result, many avant-garde Italian architects and designers looked to the exploration of the expressive possibilities of popular styling, eclecticism, kitsch, and nostalgia as a means of undermining the connotations ofcanons of taste' and elegance in the work of such mainstream designers as Vico Magistretti, Gio Ponti, and Mario Bellini. The Italian theorist, ## 126 Zanotta stand at the Eurodomus 3, Turin, featuring the Blowinflatable chair, designed by Jonathan De Pas, Donato D'Urbino, Paolo Lomazzi, and Carla Scolari, 1967 In the mid-1960s the Zanotta furniture company began to commission work from avantgarde designers, often experimenting with new materials. The Blowchair was extremely fashionable and emerged from the Pop ethos of the 1964 Biennale. Although inflatable furniture had been seen in Britain in the 1940s, it was not seriously developed until the 1960s when it was taken up by several European designers. ![](images/e4a467eaf5381dfe9dcbde0f188e9447bc8b8acd2d54613fac48df895a64c2bd.jpg) designer, and founder-member of Archizoom Associati, Andrea Branzi, subsequently described the impact of pop culture in 196os Italy: The whole of the Modern Movement's culture of design had denied consumption any autonomous value, considering it to be entirely covered by the canons of correct and rational planning. This rationality appeared to correspond to the nature of the whole industrial cycle from machine to factory to market. Now the contents of the project had to be completely altered so that the product could absorb all the mechanisms for inducement of consumption, commercial promotion and advertising communication. This meant mass languages instead of the strict canons of Rationalism; spiced up and contrived designs in place of the logical designs of the modern movement.28 Typical of this new language was the Blow inflatable chair designed by De Pas, D'Urbino, and Lomazzi for the Zanotta furniture company in 1967 [126], which embodied notions of flexibility, expendability, and the possibilities inherent in new materials. Two avant-garde groups which had an important role in what became known as the Radical Design and Anti-Design movements ## 127 Archizoom Associati Naufragio di Rose dream bed, 1967 One of a number of experimental groups associated with the Radical Design which emerged in Italy in the mid-1960s, Archizoom explored a wide range of cultural references, materials, and ideas which ran counter to the style-led dictates of mainstream furniture design in Italy. Often eclectic, their vocabulary embraced kitsch and mass-culture as well as more esoteric references. Opposed to conventional notions of 'good taste' their ideas were often communicated through the medium of exhibitions. ![](images/068c7382a742dc3d83d81917c590014081a3ce67d9232a609619dacd73798ac4.jpg) were Archizoom Associati [127] and Superstudio, both founded in Florence in 1966. Concernedwith the implications of the total environment rather than the aesthetically-charged individual object, they sought to undermine the profit-nexus of capitalism through their portrayals of a Utopian world in which the needs of everyday life were provided by self-sustaining technology, thus allowing the individual to rediscover her or his own innate creative potential. Freed (theoretically) from the constraints of conspicuous consumption and the economics of the market-place they sought, through exhibitions, manifestos, or staged environments, to explore the potential resonances of a wide range of cultural references. Other important contemporary Italian groups working along parallel lines included UFO and Gruppo 9999, both formed in Florence in 1967, and Gruppo Strum, established in Turin in the early 197os. However, in some instances, such groups did not feel that they could effect social change through involvement in the design process itself and sought to communicate their ideas through the issuing of manifestos and staging of performances. Many of the radical propositions of Italian designers in the 196os and early 197os were exhibited in the landmark exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, entitled Italy: the New Domestic Landscape. Its director was Emilio Ambasz, Curator of Design at MOMA since 1969, who had previously taught at Princeton, the Carnegie Institute of Technology, and the HfG at Ulm. He was also the editor of the substantial catalogue, which contains much that is ## 128 Ettore Sottsass Carlton Bookcase, Memphis, 1981 This striking example of Sottsass's early work for Memphis reveals a deeply anti-functionalist attitude through its premium on colour, decoration, and experimentation with form and surface. Evolving from the experimentation of the Milanese avant-garde of the late 1970s, its visual richness ran counter to the wider contemporary inclinations of furniture production which stressed elegance and refinement. extremely useful about contemporary design issues in Italy. The large exhibition was highly significant, not only for staging important debates about the sociocultural implications of design but because it marked a fundamental change of perspective for MOMA, which previously had tended to focus on the aesthetics of the individual object or celebrated designer. Ettore Sottsass Jr. played a pivotal role in this changing avant-garde climate of the late 196os and 197os, having a wealth of experience in experimental as well as mainstream industrial design. Not only had he exhibited at the first postwar Triennale in 1947, but in 1956 he worked in the studio of the American designer George Nelson, before beginning a longstanding relationship as a consultant to Olivetti in the following year. After responding to the possibilities afforded by kitsch and American Pop in the early 196os, Sottsass drew on an increasingly wide range of cultural references, exploringideas relating to meditation and love as well as reconciling aspects of ancient mythology and symbolism with imagery drawn from the contemporary world. This drawing on other cultures was partly reinforced by his visit to India in 196ı and was particularly evident in his ceramic work of the period including the Ceramics of Darkness' and the Ceramics to Shiva' series of 1963 and 1964. Like a number of his contemporaries,he also explored the status and meaning of objects in a series of furniture designs and rooms for Poltranova from the mid-196os, using the symbolism of mass culture. Furthermore, allying himself to theUtopian spirit of Radical Design he envisaged in his drawings and text for the Planet as Festival series of 1973 a world in which consumerism and the work ethic had no place but provided the launching point for a voyage of imaginative self-discovery. ## From Studio Alchymia to Memphis Studio Alchymia was founded by Alessandro and Adriana Guerriero in Milan in 1979. Its chief spokesman was the designer-writer Alessandro Mendini, and its main protagonists included EttoreSottsass Jr., Paola Navone, Andrea Branzi, and Michele de Lucchi. The practice of Alchemy' implied a pursuit of the quest to turn base substances into gold, a philosophy which evoked considerable controversy and critical attention in much of the group's work which centred on the idea of 'banality': ordinary, everyday consumer objects were transformed, or re-designed, into objects of aesthetic contemplation through the application of colour, pattern, and additional elements. Through this process they harnessed the potential of what Sottsass described asnon-cultural imagery', that is, imagery without conventional aesthetic status. Their output ranged from individual items of furniture through to total environments or performances and was often highly decorative, drawing upon references from Braun to Bauhaus and from kitsch to Kandinsky in the exploration of the communicative boundaries of design. However, as the 197os drew to a close there were increasing tensions between Mendini and Sottsass. Sottsass wished to explore the potential impact of a richer design syntax than Mendini's concerns with‘redesign' appeared to allow, as they were confined to what might be seen as the laboratory-like isolation of the experimental studio and confines of the exhibition gallery. For Sottsass the use of imagination and a rich visual language in design was both a means of enhancing the consumer experience and of persuading manufacturers to re-examine their understanding of the aesthetic possibilities inherent in everyday products. Notions of homogenization, standardization, and the production of universal models for global markets had been very much bound up in the notion of Fordism. In the Post-Fordist era, designers and manufacturers could turn their attention to the opportunities afforded by batch production, flexible manufacturing systems (FMS), or computeraided manufacture (CAM). This allowed for a greater diversity of product types and enabled producers to satisfy more easily the varied cultural inclinations and semantic values of different consumer groups. The Memphis design group was founded by Sottsass [128] and Michele De Lucchi in Milan in 1981, with the help of a Milanese cabinet-maker, Renzo Brugola, and Mario and Brunella Godani, who had a showroom. Financial backing was provided by the lighting designer and president of Artemide, Ernesto Gismondi, together with the industrialist, Fausto Celati. The group's activities and exhibitions provided a vital fulcrum for experimental designdebate for two or three years, stimulating the design world in a positive fashion. Apart from Sottsass himself none of the founder members was over 3o years of age. Like a number of other Italian twentieth-century avant-garde design groups, Memphis was originally Milan-based, but it went on to include members from other countries including Japan, the United States, Austria, Britain, and France thus becoming a standard-bearer of the New International Style', as was discussed in relation to the globalization of culture in Chapter 6. The title Memphis' has many perhaps apocryphal stories attached to it. For instance, it has been claimed by Barbara Radice, a founder member of the group, that it stemmed from the repeated playing on Sottsass's record player of a Bob Dylan song, Stick Inside of Mobile with the Memphis Blues Again. She maintained that the formative members of the group present felt that the name Memphis reflected the rich creative possibilities afforded by the ability to draw on cultural experiences of all kinds, whether the American blues, Tennessee, and rock' n' roll, or ancient Egypt and the capital of the Pharaohs. Whether or not Radice's account is entirely accurate such diverse cultural provenances contribute to the vitality of form, surface, and vocabulary associated with the group. Memphis patterns derived from the mundane printed plastic laminated surfaces of counters in suburban coffee bars, from American consumer culture, Art Deco, Hollywood or ancient civilizations; materials could range from the cheap and ordinary to the expensive; colour was another vital ingredient and, like the surface decoration deployed, was a linguistic and expressive means of indicating references to cultural experience of all kinds. The significance of Memphis lay in the ways in which many different elements came together in fresh and surprising ways, reminiscent in many ways of Isadore Ducasse/Comte de Lautréamont's Surrealist adage,the chance encounter of a sewing machine and an umbrella on a dissection table': Memphis embraced the meeting of cheap and expensive materials, of mass- and high-cultural references, of invigorating colour combinations and new forms. Furthermore, as Radice wrote in 1984: Memphis, like fashion, works on the fabric of contemporaneity, and contemporaneity means computers, electronics, videogames, science-fiction comics, Blade Runner, Space Shuttle, biogenetics, laser bombs, a new awareness of the body, exotic diets and banquets, mass exercise and tourism. Mobility is perhaps the most macroscopic novelty of this culture. Not only physical mobility but also and above all mobility of hierarchies and values; and mobility of interpretations which has liquefied the contours and solidity of things, shrinking the long, lazy waves of our 'Weltanschauung' to increasingly high frequencies until they burst and evaporate in a dust of hypotheses, in a world of events. What matters to us is not their substance but their appearance, their virtual image.29 The group worked across a range of media and products: clocks, textiles, furniture, glass, ceramics, flooring, and interiors all attracted their attention. Its members also believed that design was part of the fashion process. As the catalogue to the group's first exhibition of September 1981 stated: 'We are all sure that Memphis furniture will soon go out of style.' However, its very success ensured that many of its ideas were taken up by countless imitators, thus engendering the very commercial conformity from which its participants had sought to escape. Indeed, as one trenchant critic wrote in the late 198os: The visual promise of simplicity—though the ideological and technical bases ofMemphis designs are far from simple—has since the early eighties spawned a multitude of imitators who consider themselves to be designers'. Designers obsessed with the total objet d'art, with the renaissance of the craftsman, though they themselves have had little or no training, bodge together chairs and lamps, sofas and beds, which, as long as they are eccentric and brightly coloured, are Memphis'style. The accompanying media circus is usually more interested in the anti-bourgeois atmosphere of this design environment than in the designs per se. Hence the important and far reaching changes introduced by Memphis in the concept of design have increasingly faded into the background.30 ## The role of the crafts within the Post-Modern project For many Post-Modernists the organization of large-scale industry was perceived as a barrier to individual expression and creativity, a late twentieth-century inheritance of the long-standing tension between the constraints of mass-production and artistic integrity which had constantly resurfaced from the early phases of the Industrial Revolution. Ever since the English poet William Blake attacked Sir Joshua Reynolds's ‘world of reason' in the late eighteenth century a succession of articulate writershave attacked the spiritual andcreative consequences of the division of labour. William Morris's misgivings about many aspects of the industrialization process in the mid-nineteenth century helped sustain the enduring belief held by many that the hand-made article is superior to the machine-made, both in terms of aesthetics and function. The crafts provided an experimental arena in which new possibilities could be explored, avenues of investigation which weregenerally closed down by the structure and outlook of manufacturing industry. All Memphis pieces were, with the exception of blown glass, intended as prototypes for industrial production, and the group always allied itself to the potentiality of industrial production to produce goods on a scale capable of satisfying the respective desires and imaginations of a variety of consumers. But craft skills were seen as an important vehicle for experimentation and exploration of materials, surfaces, and forms. To this end Sottsass had brought into the Memphis circle his Milanese cabinet-making friend, Renzo Brugola, who was encouraged to help lend material substance to the new ideas of Sottsass and his colleagues. However, this emphasis on craft was not a phenomenon confined to Italy, as elsewhere in Europe and the United States in the 197os and 198os a new breedof designers redefined the boundaries and explored the visual possibilities of the crafts. In Britain in 1986, for example, John Thackera wrote about designers who had given up hope of finding sympathetic partners in industry and are exploring ways of manufacturing and distributing their own products. To some of this group the Italian experience is an inspiration; that country's success in furniture, lighting and clothing has been due, in part, to the survival of a lively artisan tradition, based in a small-scale workshop infrastructure, which makes it possible to produce, in small batches, products which could not economically be made in huge factories.³1 ## Post-Modernism: the wider picture Reaction against the semantic limitations of modernism was not restricted to industrial design, the decorative and applied arts, and architecture [129].Similar experimentation in typography,letterspacing, and the expressive possibilities of photolithography could be ## 129 Hans Hollein Interior of the Austrian Travel Centre, Vienna, 1976–8 This striking interior is a potent expression of Post-Modernist values. Many of the elements of the interior allude appropriately to references of travel, exoticism, and far-away destinations, including metal palm trees, a golden-roofed tempietto, and the railing and lifebuoy of an ocean liner. ![](images/4a7e2a36ded2a3343df4ba62014e30168b9ad7ab9908bb8577f0bb55d467a52d.jpg) seen in the work of the influential graphic designer Wolfgang Weingart who, having reacted against the studied clarity of Swiss International Style typography, became associated with American New Wave design in the 197os [130, 131]. Such an emphasis on individualexpression was taken up by April Greiman, a leading figure in such developments in California in the late 197os and 198os,32 and others associated with the style magazine Emigré, launched by Rudy VanderLans in Berkeley in 1982. Similar tendencies can be discerned in the graphic work of Javier Mariscal inSpain, although his work also extended into other design media such astextiles, lighting, interiors, and furniture, in connection with which Ettore Sottsass invited him to participate in the Memphis exhibition of 1981. A radical spirit could also be discerned in British street-style magazines such as i-D, published, edited, and art-directed by Terry Jones from 198o, and The Face, art-directed by Neville Brody between 1981 and 1986. Both designers were highly influential in their abandonment of conventional grid-base layouts, combining all kinds of surface marks with varieties of type and letter-forms and exploring the expressive possibilities of different textures and decorative motifs. Initially motivated by the vitality and crudeness of Punk, Neville Brody, in the eclectic manner of post-modern design, also drew upon the collagiste, photomontage, and typographic experimentation of Dada, Russian Constructivism, the Bauhaus, De Stijl, and other avant-garde trends of interwar modernism as a means of revitalizing the page. In keeping with the design cultism of the 198os his work was celebrated in an exhibition entitled The Graphic Language of Neville Brody33at the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, in 1988 and has been extremely influential [132]: pale imitations of much of his early 198os works were incorporated into the signage and design of many fashionable shops, record stores, packaging, and magazines. He has been commissioned by many important clients in Europe, the United States and the Far
# RA NO.3 \$4.00 THE GRAPHIX MAGAZINE THAT LOST ITS FAITH IN NIHILISM ## 130 Gary Panter Rawmagazine cover, no.3,1981 The crude, brash styling of this cover marks it out as a manifestation of the experimental climate of the late 1970s and 1980s. Like much New Wave American graphic design of the time it represented a reaction against conventional, carefully structured approaches to typography and layout. ## 131 Tom van den Haspel and Henk Elenga Front cover of Lecturis, 1981 Both designers were members of the Hard Werken design group which has become renowned for experimentation and freedom in graphic communication. Designers associated with the group have explored combinations of surface, image, and typography in an invigorating fashion. East—Japanese retailers such as Men's Bigi and Parco, Dutch Telecom, PTT, Bloomingdales in New York, and the Body Shop in England—reinforcing the concept of global potency of style in affluent industrialized societies. ## Pop, punk, and Post-Modernism: an afterword Pop in the early 196os has often been interpreted as a youthful challenge to many traditionally accepted values,34 and the vibrant, expendable consumer values that it furthered were not seen as a serious threat to the social status quo. However, from 1966, when hallucinogenic drugs, free love, and interest in eastern religions assumed an increasingly significant profile, the outlook began to change. Psychedelic patterns and imagery, associated with vividly colourful experience of ![](images/e099f8a36b227ce66882baebff413fa9c42670555889c345e892b6064502e744.jpg) ![](images/dd07f91eb86b561f5e158f59dd3aaae73f9a8871797a69289f39a50ec329f22d.jpg) LSD, appeared widely in posters, record covers, clothing and other surfaces, including shop fronts. Originating in West Coast America Psychedelic art was associated with alternative or ‘hippy' lifestyles and found expression in the widely disseminated posters of Rick Griffin, Wes Wilson, and Victor Moscoso. Their counterparts in Britain included Martin Sharp, illustrator for the notorious magazine Oz,35 and the partnership of Nigel Weymouth and Michael English (known as Hapsash and the Coloured Coat), best known for their mural and shop-frontwork. However, any perceived social or cultural threat which such design might be seen to embody was undermined by the high levels of commercialization of the style, which ceased to embrace any genuine fundamentals of an alternative lifestyle as soon as it became readily available off-the-peg' in a wide variety of retail outlets. A similar transformation can be seen to have taken place with Punk, ## 132 Neville Brody Brochure cover for FontFont 5, Fontshop International, 1992 The first FontShop was set up in Germany in 1989 in the belief that digital typefaces could be more successfully developed by designers themselves rather than by a limited number of major companies which were unwilling to accommodate radical design solutions. In 1990 Brody established FontWorks UK, part of an expanding international franchising network which invigorated the global typographic imagination much as radical young designers had the appearance of independent record covers more than a decade earlier. which some writers have seen as an affirmation of the working-class urban reality of unemployment, expressed through ripped, zipped, and 'dirty' dress that was ‘the sartorial equivalent of swear words', or personal ornamentation and body-piercing associated with overtones of deviancy'. Ideas and information about music and events were communicated crudely through small-scalenewsheets'. Often typed with hand-written deletions and insertions and photocopied such fanzines were stapled together and produced invery small runs for local networks: better known examples includeSniffin Glue and Ripped and Torn which began in 1976. The impact of such work has been significant and within five years became a mainstream element of commercialized street style in the graphic work of Jamie Reid, Michael Garret, Peter Saville, and Neville Brody. The immediate impact of Punk's outcry against the establishment was relatively short-lived as offensiveness'was soon incorporated into mainstream cultural expression, with ripped and torn clothing soon mass-produced and available in fashionable boutiques. None the less, as a number of writers have argued, it did reassert Britain as a centre for new and original ideas in design. But the rapid move from innovation to orthodoxy was not confined to street style. Many critics also drew attention to the ways in which positive and conscious moves to enrich the design and architectural vocabulary, as seen in the origins of the New International Style', might become devalued in what might be termed ‘simplistic, reachme-down formulae'. For example, in the book accompanying The Design Now exhibition in Frankfurt in 1988, Volker Fischer wrote of such formulae: At three or four removes they may degenerate into a new form of kitsch, easy on the eye, tailor made for the suburban bungalow, with oriels and columnettes adorning facades across the land! Post-Modernism is basically characterised by the rediscovery of ornament, colour, symbolic connections and the treasure trove of the history of form.36 ![](images/6ba6b666f7bc873baa3e9483c93ff7c1cb72ce5879ee80565f8b840ad3608648.jpg)
